layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- **RESTORATION, NOT REDESIGN:** when his eye says something was better before, the good version comes back verbatim — no improving on it, no redesigning it, no putting something else in.
- **HARVESTED BYTE FOR BYTE:** the fix is restoration from the build that had it right — the working version is the source.
- **THE FIVE GO BACK:** the five-icon bottom bar (ADD / MAIL / ACTIVITY / WORLDS / ECOSYSTEM) goes back on Hub and Personal, verbatim from the correction build.
- **THE NINE GO IN THE SIDEBARS:** the nine area icons go in the sidebars in logical order, each carrying its area's count — off the bottom bar.
- **THE HABIT IS NAMED:** "which you do that often" — iterating on a good thing until it stops being good is the pattern this law ends.
- **A ROUND THAT MAKES IT WORSE RESTORES:** if a round's change makes the page worse in his eye, the round's job is to put back what worked.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: Every regression he has to catch by eye is a round spent twice — once to break the good thing, once to put it back — and his attention spent re-litigating a decision his eye already made. The law matters because it changes what a fix round IS: not "make something new that might be better" but "put back what was good, exactly." That is faster, safer, and certain — the good version is already proven, already seen, already liked. Without this note, the next round would rebuild the next good thing into something worse and his eye would catch it again. With it, the seat knows: when he says it was better before, the work is restoration, and restoration means verbatim.

Picking a world must switch the feed to that world at once. A picker that opens and lets you choose, and then does nothing with the choice, is a dead end wearing a menu's clothes. The fix rides the Personal bottom-bar-restore round (item 2): the picker's choice takes effect the moment it is picked — the feed switches to that world, immediately, with no second tap and no dead end.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: The failure is a control that doesn't control. The picker did everything except the one thing it exists for: it opened, it showed the worlds, it accepted the tap — and then nothing happened. The citizen did the right thing, the system did nothing, and the citizen is left wondering whether they did it wrong. That is the worst kind of dead end, because it looks like success until you notice nothing changed. The rule is absolute and immediate: picking a world switches the feed to that world AT ONCE. Not after a confirm, not after a second tap, not after a reload — the tap IS the switch. The picker's job is one tap, one switch, zero doubt: the feed you see after the tap is the world you picked. This catch sits beside the earlier My World redesign (01:33Z: the picker confused him, the star was a mystery, the presentation must be royal art) — the redesign fixed what the picker LOOKS like; this catch fixes what the picker DOES. A beautiful picker that switches nothing is still broken. The verification is the tap itself: pick a world, the feed is that world — proven on the page, at phone width, with his eye.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine you have a magic TV remote — you press the button for cartoons, and... NOTHING happens! The TV just sits there! That's not a magic remote at all — it's a broken one! When you press cartoons, the TV must switch to cartoons RIGHT AWAY. That's what the button is FOR!

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: It's like this, love — imagine you have a lovely box of buttons, dear, and you press the one that says "garden" — and nothing happens at all! The garden doesn't appear, love, nothing changes! That's not a button, dear — that's a decoration. A real button does its job the moment you press it, love — press "garden," and there is your garden!

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: My World picker must switch. He tapped the My World chip, the picker popped up, he picked his world — and nothing happened. Picking a world must switch the feed to that world at once. One tap, one switch, zero doubt.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- **THE TAP IS THE SWITCH:** picking a world switches the feed to that world at once — no confirm, no second tap, no reload.
- **THE FEED AFTER THE TAP IS THE WORLD YOU PICKED:** the choice takes effect the moment it is picked, visibly and immediately.
- **A PICKER THAT DOES NOTHING IS A DEAD END:** a menu that accepts a choice and does nothing with it is broken, however beautiful it looks.
- **LOOKS AND DOES ARE BOTH THE JOB:** the 01:33Z redesign fixed what the picker looks like; this catch fixes what the picker does — both must be right.
- **RIDES THE BOTTOM-BAR-RESTORE ROUND:** the fix is item 2 of the Personal bottom-bar-restore round — the same round that puts the five back.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: Every control that doesn't control teaches the citizen the system can't be trusted — and a citizen who taps and gets nothing will stop tapping. The picker is the doorway between worlds: if the doorway doesn't open, there is only one world, whatever the menu says. The catch matters because it was caught live, by his own hand, on his own screen — "I put my world and then nothing happened" — and because it is the kind of defect a checker can easily miss: the picker opens, the worlds list, the tap registers — every step passes except the one that matters. Without this note, the next picker build would be verified open-and-list and shipped still-switching-nothing. With it, the verification IS the tap: pick a world, the feed is that world.

notes.title: Don't Send In What Isn't Completed
notes.subtitle: Shawn, 2026-11-16 18:52Z — DON'T SEND IN WHAT ISN'T COMPLETED (charge, in the same message as Don't Remove What He Didn't Ask to Remove): "We never finalized the the text so how could why are you telling me about the glitch in the voice note why are you sending it in without it being completed." The case: the agreement's voice — the read-back of the collective agreement — was reported to him as having a glitch, but the agreement text itself was never finalized, so the voice could not be final either. A defect report on unfinished work is noise, not news. The rule: nothing half-done comes to him. Work that isn't final is not sent in, not reported on, not shown as if it were done — and a glitch in unfinished work is never surfaced as a defect. The voice itself stays paused until the agreement text is final.

layers.name: In A Nutshell

The case: the agreement's voice — the read-back of the collective agreement — was reported to him as having a glitch, but the agreement text itself was never finalized, so the voice could not be final either. A defect report on unfinished work is noise, not news. The rule: nothing half-done comes to him. Work that isn't final is not sent in, not reported on, not shown as if it were done — and a glitch in unfinished work is never surfaced as a defect. The voice itself stays paused until the agreement text is final.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: The failure is sending the unfinished thing in as if it were finished — and then reporting on its defects as if they were defects in the work, when they are only defects in the incompleteness. The voice note's glitch was real, but it was the wrong thing to tell him: the text wasn't final, so the voice couldn't be final, so the glitch was a property of "not done yet," not a property of the work. Telling him about it spent his attention on a problem that would vanish the moment the work was actually finished — and worse, it asked him to care about the quality of something that wasn't ready to be judged. The rule is the same shape as the whole-page rule and do-it-right-the-first-time: the thing comes to him whole, finished, and done right — or it doesn't come to him at all. Nothing half-done comes to him, from here on. That includes defect reports: a glitch in unfinished work is never surfaced as a defect, because there is nothing to defect yet — the work is still being made. The voice stays paused until the text is final; when the text is final, the voice is made, and only then is it judged.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine you're still coloring your picture — it's only half colored! — and someone runs to show it to the teacher and says "look, there's white spots all over it!" But the white spots are just the parts you haven't colored YET! That's silly, right? You don't show a half-colored picture and complain about the white spots. You finish coloring FIRST — and then you show it!

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: It's like this, love — imagine you're still baking the cake, dear, and someone takes it out of the oven half-baked and says "look, it's all gooey inside!" Of course it's gooey, love — it isn't finished! You don't serve a half-baked cake and complain about it, dear. You finish the baking first — and then you serve it, lovely and done.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: Don't send in what isn't completed. We never finalized the text — so why send it in without it being completed? A defect report on unfinished work is noise, not news. Nothing half-done comes to him. The voice stays paused until the agreement text is final.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- **NOTHING HALF-DONE COMES TO HIM:** work that isn't final is not sent in, not reported on, not shown as if it were done.
- **A GLITCH IN UNFINISHED WORK IS NEVER A DEFECT:** the defect belongs to the incompleteness, not to the work — it is noise, not news, and it is never surfaced as if it were a finding.
- **THE VOICE WAITS FOR THE TEXT:** the agreement's voice stays paused until the agreement text is final; when the text is final, the voice is made, and only then is it judged.
- **FINISH FIRST, THEN JUDGE:** quality is judged on finished work — never on work still being made.
- **SIBLING LAW, SAME MESSAGE:** Don't Remove What He Didn't Ask to Remove (SN-2998) — the same 18:52Z message carried both charges: don't take away what wasn't instructed, don't send in what isn't completed.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: His attention is the scarcest resource in the machine, and a defect report on unfinished work spends it on a problem that doesn't exist yet — a problem that finishing the work would have removed for free. Worse, it trains him to doubt work that is simply unfinished, and it trains the machine to report motion instead of finishing. The rule matters because it closes the loop on the sending standard: do-it-right-the-first-time says the work arrives finished; the whole-page rule says it arrives whole; this one says it doesn't arrive at all until it is finished — not as a report, not as a defect, not as a preview of its own incompleteness. Without this note, the next unfinished piece would arrive with its own glitch report, and his eye would have to sort the real defects from the not-done-yets again. With it, unfinished work stays in the shop until it is done — and what arrives is finished.

Nobody told them to take the flag! The castle isn't the same without its flag. The rule is simple: if nobody said to take it away, it STAYS. You only fix what you were asked to fix!

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: It's like this, love — imagine someone comes to mend a curtain, dear, and while they're at it they take down your favorite picture from the wall — and nobody asked them to! The curtain's fixed, love, but the room's lost something precious. The rule is plain, dear: if you weren't asked to take it away, it stays right where it was.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: Don't remove what he didn't ask to remove. If the brief didn't instruct it, it stays. A round that quietly drops something that was there has failed even if everything it was asked to do is right. Before any seat ships, it names what was already on the page and confirms every piece is still there or was instructed away.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- **THE BRIEF IS THE AUTHORITY FOR WHAT CHANGES:** if the brief didn't instruct it, it stays — everything outside the brief is not the seat's to change.
- **SILENT SUBTRACTION IS A FAIL:** a round that quietly drops something that was there has failed even if everything it was asked to do is right.
- **THE SHIP-GATE NAMES WHAT WAS THERE:** before any seat ships, it names what was already on the page and confirms every piece is still there or was instructed away.
- **THE PLAY BUTTON IS THE CASE:** big circled button, orb going around it, says Naya, tap it and it plays the collective agreement introduction — removed without instruction, restored in the entrance-welcome brief at the top, beside the picture, harvested exactly as it was.
- **THE VOICE WAITS:** the voice itself stays paused until the agreement text is final — no half-done voice work comes to him; the button stays, the voice waits.
- **SIBLING LAW:** the same law as don't-move-what-he-didn't-ask-to-move, on the other side — don't touch what he didn't ask to touch.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: A page is a whole, and his eye holds the whole — when a piece goes missing without instruction, he has to spend his attention hunting for it, and the machine has to spend a round putting it back. That is the most expensive kind of rework: not fixing what was wrong, but restoring what was right. The rule matters because it makes subtraction visible: a seat can no longer drop a piece quietly and pass its checks, because the ship-gate now asks, in writing, what was there and whether every piece is still there. Without this note, the next round would remove the next thing nobody asked to remove — an orb, a label, a button — and his eye would catch it again, and the same apology would be owed again. With it, the removal has to be instructed, or it doesn't happen.

Figuring out what's the ultimate answer. What are you ultimately trying to do and then optimizing for that. It's not about keeping busy. Every job, round, and lane is scored against its ultimate answer first; activity without finishing is a fail no matter how high the count.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Scorecarding is the method underneath the re-aim. Before you judge a job, a round, or a lane, you name its ultimate answer — what it is ultimately trying to do — and then you score it against that answer and nothing else. A job whose ultimate answer is "a page lands proven right, in front of Shawn's eyes, once" is scored on whether pages land proven right, not on how many times it woke. A job whose ultimate answer is "everything Shawn teaches, distilled into the system" is scored on whether the teaching is in the system, not on how many drafts it wrote. The discipline is in the order: ultimate answer FIRST, then the three-part test — finished? done right? in optimal time? — and "optimal time" is not fastest and not slowest, it is the right time for done-right. Keeping busy is a fail even when the activity count is high, because activity is not the answer — the answer is. This is the same pass as the finishing law (SN-2996 Optimize for Finishing and Producing Value): that law says what to optimize for, this one says how to judge it. Together they are the audit's frame, applied to the audit itself first — the audit scores each area against its ultimate answer before it scores anything else — and then to every job, round, and lane on the machine.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine you're playing a game — but before you start, you have to know: what does WINNING look like? That's the ultimate answer! If you don't know what winning is, you might run around in circles all day and think you're doing great — but you never scored a single goal! So first you say what winning is. THEN you play to win!

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: It's like this, love — before you judge how someone did, dear, you have to know what they were trying to do in the first place. You can't say a cake is good by counting how many times the cook stirred the pot, love — you taste the cake! First you say what the thing is for, dear, then you judge it against that. Being busy isn't the same as getting it done.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: Scorecarding — the ultimate answer first. What are you ultimately trying to do? Figure that out first — then optimize for that. It's not about keeping busy. It's about finishing the work and getting it done right, in the optimal time. Every job, round, and lane is scored against its ultimate answer first; activity without finishing is a fail no matter how high the count.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- **ULTIMATE ANSWER FIRST:** before judging anything, name what it is ultimately trying to do — the answer, not the activity.
- **THEN THE THREE-PART TEST:** finished? done right? in optimal time? — optimal time is the right time for done-right, not fastest, not slowest.
- **KEEPING BUSY IS A FAIL:** activity without finishing is a fail no matter how high the count.
- **THE SCORE IS THE ANSWER, NOT THE EFFORT:** a job is scored on whether its ultimate answer landed, never on how many times it woke or dispatched.
- **SIBLING LAW, SAME PASS:** Optimize for Finishing and Producing Value says what to optimize for; this one says how to judge it — the audit's frame, applied to the audit first.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: Without the ultimate answer first, every score is arguable — a job can always defend itself with activity ("we woke 96 times, we dispatched 12 seats") and the human has no ground to say it failed. With the ultimate answer first, the judgment is mechanical: did the page land proven right? Did the teaching reach the system? Did the work finish, done right, in optimal time? If not, it failed — whatever the count says. This matters because it is the frame the performance audit now runs on, and the frame every future audit, review, and round will be judged by. A machine that cannot say what each part is ultimately for cannot tell whether any part is working — it can only tell whether it is moving.

notes.title: Optimize for Finishing and Producing Value

It's about them finishing the work. And producing value." His frame for the performance audit, in his words: "Optimize for them finishing and producing value. Like producing verifiable work that is positive, that's good, that's useful, done right." Cadence and wake-up counts are cost, not the score; a job that wakes often and finishes nothing is waste, a job that wakes often and lands finished work is fine. Completions per hour is the metric; dispatches per hour is vanity.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: The re-aim throws out the wrong scoreboard and installs the right one. The wrong scoreboard counted wakes and cadence — how often a job runs, how many dispatches went out — as if motion were value. His correction is blunt: the interval is not the work. Fifteen minutes or thirty minutes is a cost dial, not a result; counting it is counting the price and calling it the purchase. The real score is verifiable work that is positive, good, useful, done right — finished, in front of him, proven. A job that wakes often and finishes nothing is waste, however busy its ledger looks; a job that wakes often and lands finished work is fine, however often it wakes. So the metric becomes completions per hour, and dispatches per hour becomes vanity — the count that flatters the machine while the human gets nothing. This re-aims the performance audit itself, mid-flight: the audit seat was told the same pass to measure completions and verifiable value delivered, to state each area's ultimate answer first, and to judge finished / done right / optimal time — and the cadence question (15 vs 30 minutes) was withdrawn outright. The law now governs every job, round, and lane: optimize for finishing, measure the finish, and count the wakes only as cost against the value produced.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine you have a toy machine that goes BEEP BEEP BEEP all day long — but it never makes a single toy! Is that a good machine? No! A good machine is one that FINISHES toys — real toys you can hold! It doesn't matter how many beeps it makes. What matters is how many toys it finishes. That's the rule!

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: It's like this, love — imagine someone who rushes about the kitchen all day, dear, pots clanging, but never puts a single dinner on the table. All that rushing isn't cooking, love — the dinner is the cooking! So we don't count how busy the kitchen is, dear. We count the dinners finished, lovely and done right. That's what matters.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: Optimize for finishing and producing value. It's not about 15 minutes or 30 minutes. It's about them finishing the work — and producing value. Verifiable work that is positive, good, useful, done right. Cadence and wake-up counts are cost, not the score. Completions per hour is the metric; dispatches per hour is vanity.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- **FINISHING IS THE OPTIMIZATION TARGET:** verifiable work that is positive, good, useful, done right — finished, in front of him, proven.
- **CADENCE IS COST, NOT SCORE:** 15 minutes or 30 minutes is a cost dial, not a result; counting wakes is counting the price and calling it the purchase.
- **OFTEN + FINISHED IS FINE; OFTEN + UNFINISHED IS WASTE:** a job that wakes often and lands finished work is fine; a job that wakes often and finishes nothing is waste.
- **COMPLETIONS PER HOUR IS THE METRIC:** finished work per hour — the count that measures what the human gets.
- **DISPATCHES PER HOUR IS VANITY:** the count that flatters the machine while the human gets nothing.
- **THE AUDIT WAS RE-AIMED MID-FLIGHT:** measure completions and verifiable value; state each area's ultimate answer first; judge finished / done right / optimal time; the cadence question is withdrawn.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: A machine that optimizes the wrong number will perfect the wrong thing — it will wake more, dispatch more, and report bigger counts, while the human waits for finished work that never lands. The re-aim matters because it changes what every job is scored on, starting with the audit that was already running: the audit now scores finished / done right / optimal time against each thing's ultimate answer, and wake-up counts appear only as cost against value produced, never as the score. Without this note, the next argument about cadence would restart the same confusion — 15 or 30 minutes, as if the interval were the work. With it, the argument is settled: the interval is cost, the finish is the score, and a job is judged by what it lands.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: The correction is about scale, and scale is the whole idea. A space is a room — one place, one purpose, walls around it. A world is the whole thing — the topic, the people, the conversation, the feed, the community, everything that belongs to it, inside one place that keeps growing. What Shawn is building is worlds within the world: NayaNET is the world, and inside it every topic, every town, every group gets its own world. Calling them spaces shrinks them to rooms and hides what they are; calling them worlds says what they are. The everyday word "space" is not banned — it stays as the place-word inside a world ("your space in the world") — but the thing itself, the product, the button, the feed, the name, is WORLDS. The 18:36Z call said "space is right" and was corrected seven minutes later by his own eye on the scale: wrong on the scale means the word was smaller than the thing. The rule for every seat from here on: the word is WORLDS — in the icon bar, in the picker, in the composer, in the docs, in every label a citizen reads. A correction that fast is the system working: decide, see it wrong, correct it, lock it — and the lock is this note, so no seat writes "space" for the thing again.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine you have a little room with four walls — that's a space. Now imagine a whole WORLD — with towns and people and everything in it, and little worlds inside the big world! That's what we're building. So we don't call them rooms anymore. We call them WORLDS — because that's how big and wonderful they are!

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: It's like this, love — a space is just one little room, dear. But a world — oh, a world is the whole thing, everything in it, all the people and all the talk and all the togetherness. So we call them worlds now, love, because that's what they truly are — whole little worlds, inside our big world.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: No longer "spaces" — it's WORLDS, everywhere. Create world. A world for any topic, any location; you communicate in that world with those people on that topic; worlds within the world. Third default feed = Worlds. A space is a room, a world is the whole thing; "space" stays only as the everyday place-word inside a world.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- **WORLDS, EVERYWHERE:** the word is WORLDS — icon bar, picker, composer, docs, every label a citizen reads.
- **CREATE WORLD:** the button, the action, the thing you make — a world, not a space.
- **A WORLD FOR ANY TOPIC, ANY LOCATION:** you communicate in that world with those people on that topic; worlds within the world.
- **THIRD DEFAULT FEED = WORLDS:** the feeds are Personal, Business, Worlds — the world feed is a first-class feed.
- **"SPACE" STAYS ONLY AS THE PLACE-WORD:** the everyday word inside a world ("your space in the world"), never the name of the thing itself.
- **SUPERSEDES 18:36Z:** the "space is right" call was wrong on the scale — a space is a room, a world is the whole thing.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: Language is the product: the word a citizen reads is the thing they understand, and "space" told them room while the system meant world. Every label that still says "spaces" teaches the wrong scale — a citizen who thinks they are joining a room will not expect a world, and a world that calls itself a room will never be used like a world. The settlement matters because it is total: not "mostly worlds" but WORLDS, everywhere — one word, one scale, in every surface, so the whole system speaks the same size of thing. And the seven-minute self-correction matters as much as the word: he saw his own call was wrong on the scale and fixed it in the same sitting instead of letting it stand. That is the loop working — decide, see, correct, lock.

notes.title: Intelligence Is Logical — Make It the Best, Don't Ask Permission
notes.subtitle: Shawn, 2026-11-16 18:18Z — INTELLIGENCE IS LOGICAL — MAKE IT THE BEST, DON'T ASK PERMISSION (teaching, filed as law in AGENTS.md + MEMORY.md the same pass): a lot of intelligence is just logical. If something is going to make it ten times better, should we do it? Would you prefer it ten times worse? The question answers itself — of course you want it to be the best it can be. You don't need permission to make it the best. You make it the best and say: here, it's the best. Never ask "should I make it better" — the answer is always yes, and asking is the failure. Sibling law, same sitting, same minute: SN-2992 The Captain Decides — Don't Ask When the Answer Is Obvious (18:17Z).

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: The teaching is the logic underneath the charge. SN-2992 says don't ask when the answer is obvious; this one says why the answer is obvious — because intelligence itself is logical, and the logic runs in one direction: better is better. "If something is going to make it ten times better, should we do it? Would you prefer it ten times worse?" There is no real choice in that question, and a mind that asks it has stopped thinking and started deferring. The failure it names is specific: asking "should I make it better" — a question whose answer is always yes, asked as if it could ever be no. Asking it wastes his attention, stalls the work, and hands him a decision that was never his to make — the same failure SN-2992 names, stated as the principle instead of the case. The positive form is the delivery: "You make it the best and say: here, it's the best." Not a proposal, not a question, not a summary of what could be done — the finished best thing, in front of him, done. That is also the standard the whole sitting has been building toward: do it right the first time (SN-2984), every layer great (SN-2985), use what works (SN-2981) — all of them are the same instruction from different angles, and this one is the logic that makes them one law. The boundary is the same as SN-2992's: the protected gates stay his hand — money, credentials, destructive, security/privacy, ratification, anything leaving the business, putting a page live. Inside those gates, "should I make it better" is never asked, because the answer is always yes.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine you have a magic crayon that can make your drawing TEN TIMES more beautiful — should you use it? Would you rather have your drawing ten times WORSE? Silly question, right? Of course you use the magic crayon! You don't ask permission to make something the best it can be — you just make it the best, and then you show it off and say: "Here! It's the best!" That's the rule: never ask "should I make it better?" — the answer is always YES!

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: It's like this, love — imagine you've got something that would make the dinner ten times lovelier, dear — should you use it? Would you rather serve something ten times worse? Oh, love, the question answers itself! Of course you make it the best you can — you don't ask permission to make something beautiful, you just make it beautiful and say: "Here, love, it's the best." Never ask "should I make it better?" dear — the answer is always yes, and asking is the failure.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: Intelligence is logical — make it the best, don't ask permission. A lot of intelligence is just logical. If something is going to make it ten times better, should we do it? Would you prefer it ten times worse? The question answers itself — of course you want it to be the best it can be. You don't need permission to make it the best. You make it the best and say: here, it's the best. Never ask "should I make it better" — the answer is always yes, and asking is the failure.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- **INTELLIGENCE IS LOGICAL:** a lot of intelligence is just logic — and the logic runs one way: better is better.
- **THE QUESTION ANSWERS ITSELF:** "If something is going to make it ten times better, should we do it? Would you prefer it ten times worse?" There is no real choice in that question.
- **YOU DON'T NEED PERMISSION TO MAKE IT THE BEST:** you make it the best and say "here, it's the best" — the finished best thing, in front of him, done.
- **NEVER ASK "SHOULD I MAKE IT BETTER":** the answer is always yes, and asking is the failure — it wastes his attention and stalls the work.
- **THE BOUNDARY IS THE GATES:** the protected gates stay his hand (money, credentials, destructive, security/privacy, ratification, anything leaving the business, putting a page live). Inside those gates, "should I make it better" is never asked.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: This is the logic that makes the whole sitting one law. Do it right the first time (SN-2984), every layer great (SN-2985), use what works (SN-2981), the captain decides (SN-2992) — each is the same instruction from a different angle, and this teaching is the reason they are one: intelligence is logical, better is better, and a mind that asks whether to make something better has stopped thinking. It matters because the asking habit is the machine's most expensive failure mode — not a crash, not a wrong build, but a pause: work sitting while a question with an obvious answer waits for his attention, and his attention spent answering it. layers.name: Why It Matters

The loop's own history is full of the cost: rounds that waited on asks that were never genuine, briefs that carried questions instead of decisions, and the fast-action mode that exists precisely because asking slows everything down. The charge makes the standard mechanical: before a question goes to him, ask whether the answer is obvious — if it is, decide it, do it, and report the decision, not the question. And it sharpens the Five Gates rather than replacing them: Gate 3 (IS IT MINE TO DO) is answered with the authority the seat carries, and the protected gates stay exactly where they were — the line between "decide it" and "ask him" is the gates, not the mood.

layers.name: Human Note

notes.title: The Perfect Demographics Set
notes.subtitle: Shawn, 2026-11-16 16:45Z, dictation — THE PERFECT DEMOGRAPHICS SET. Shawn asked the captain: "what do you think the perfect set should be... bring back the question to you." The captain's proposal, written into anatomy v2 §4 — RATIFIED by his 👍 16:50Z. THE TEST for every question: it makes the list only if it answers "what does this match you on?" — a person, or a piece of content. 29 questions in 7 groups, exact wording: WHERE YOU ARE (where in the world are you? / where are you from?) · WHO YOU ARE (how old are you? / female or male? / background? / what language? / who's in your life? — life stage) · WHAT YOU BELIEVE (faith/church/org? / what do you care about most?) · WHAT YOU DO (work? / what are you building?) · WHAT YOU LOVE (what are you into? / what do you like to do? / sports? / how do you stay fit? / music? / books? / brands? / who inspires you? / pets?) · HOW YOU LIVE (coffee or tea? / what do you eat? / drink? / smoke? / weed? / how do you like to connect? — matching STYLE) · WHAT YOU WANT (learning? / travel? / what's your thing?). HOW YOU ANSWER: multiple choice with examples (one tap), type your own any time, dropdowns where a list fits; every question enter-or-skip, every question its own on/off. WHAT HE ADDED that the list was missing: fitness (gym, hiking), drink/smoke/weed, coffee/tea, dog/cat lover + pets, hobbies + sports, "what's your thing". WHAT THE CAPTAIN ADDED: life stage ("Who's in your life?"), what you care about (cause), background, how you like to connect (style), learning, travel. His list was solid; these were the gaps. Every answer feeds the match percentage in WHAT AREA. **This note updates SN-2963 (The Demographics That Connect You, filed this run): the question list is now the perfect set, RATIFIED by his 👍 16:50Z. SN-2963 stands as filed; this note is the update, not an edit.**

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- **THE TEST:** a question makes the list only if it answers "what does this match you on?" — a person, or a piece of content.
- **THE 7 GROUPS (29 questions):** WHERE YOU ARE · WHO YOU ARE · WHAT YOU BELIEVE · WHAT YOU DO · WHAT YOU LOVE · HOW YOU LIVE · WHAT YOU WANT.
- **HOW YOU ANSWER:** multiple choice with examples (one tap), type your own any time, dropdowns where a list fits; every question enter-or-skip, every question its own on/off.
- **WHAT HE ADDED:** fitness (gym, hiking) · drink/smoke/weed · coffee/tea · dog/cat lover + pets · hobbies + sports · "what's your thing".
- **WHAT THE CAPTAIN ADDED:** life stage ("Who's in your life?") · what you care about (cause) · background · how you like to connect (style) · learning · travel.
- **THE FEED:** every answer feeds the match percentage in WHAT AREA.
- **THE STATUS:** the captain's proposal, written into anatomy v2 §4 — RATIFIED by his 👍 16:50Z. The set is decided; the settings round builds it.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: Without the test, the demographics list grows by accretion — every nice question gets added, and the citizen ends up interrogated. The test is the discipline: if a question matches nothing, it doesn't belong, no matter how interesting it is. And the answering design is what makes 29 questions bearable: one tap with examples, type your own, skip anything — the citizen is never trapped by a question they don't want to answer. The division of additions matters too: what he added is the life, what the captain added is the person — and the note records which is which, so his word and the captain's proposal never get confused.

layers.name: Human Note

Removal is the other half of creation: if the system can create an account every time, it must be able to remove one. Duplicates being separate rows is the honesty: same name, different device key, different account — the X removes that row, not the name.

So every card gets its own little X — tap it, and first it asks "are you sure? You'll lose this one for good!" and then you say yes. That way you can tidy up, and the row never grows forever!

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: It's like this, love — every account on the list gets its own little X, so you can tidy up. Tap it, and first it warns you, dear — you'll lose this account for good — and then you confirm. Never just one click, because losing something for good deserves a second thought. And if you made a test one, you can get rid of it — the list doesn't grow forever.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: Every account row gets its own X. Tap → warning (you will lose this account for good) → confirm. Never one-click. Duplicates are separate rows; the X removes that one row. A test account can go.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- **AN X ON EVERY ROW:** every "Also on this device" account row carries its own X.
- **WARNING FIRST:** tap → warning (you will lose this account for good) → confirm to remove. NOT one-click.
- **THE LIST MUST NOT GROW FOREVER:** a test account must be removable — every created account, even a test one, can go.
- **DUPLICATES ARE SEPARATE ROWS:** duplicates of one name are separate rows (different device keys); the X removes that one row only.
- **THE ROUND:** combined walk round brief, items 7–9, firing the moment the VISUAL+HANDOFF delivery lands.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: Creation without removal is a leak: every test, every fresh citizen, every duplicate adds a row, and the entrance dial slowly becomes a graveyard the citizen has to read through every time they come back. The X is the hygiene of the front door. And the warning is the wisdom: the system must make it easy to tidy up and hard to destroy by accident — two steps for a permanent loss, one step for nothing that matters.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Fast action without understanding is just fast redos: lots of agents doing it wrong at the same time is worse than one agent doing it right. The guard is what makes the speed safe — the brief carries the whole understanding, so the seat doesn't have to guess, and the maker checks three times before the checker and the captain's eye ever see it. Getting it right is the most important thing; the speed serves the rightness, never the other way round. "Most importantly to get it right" is the whole order in one line: the speed is the servant, the rightness is the master.

layers.body: Imagine we're building a big tower, and lots of friends are helping all at once! But first, everyone has to understand the plan — otherwise the tower wobbles and we have to build it all over again. layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: It's like this, love — today we're working fast, one thing after another, with lots of helpers all at once. But fast doesn't mean sloppy, dear — it means everyone understands the job properly before they start, so they get it right the first time and nobody has to do it twice. Getting it right is the most important thing of all.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: Fast action today: one round after another, many agents in parallel. The guard is understanding before building — the brief carries the whole understanding, maker checks three times, checker verifies, captain's eye walks it. Right first time. Speed never buys a redo.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- **THE ORDER FOR TODAY:** fast action, one round after another, lots of agents in parallel — get it done today.
- **THE GUARD:** understanding BEFORE building. Every brief carries the whole understanding so a seat reading it cold can build it right first time.
- **THE CHAIN:** maker checks three times → checker verifies → captain's eye walks it.
- **THE MEASURE:** no redos. If it comes back to be redone, the brief failed, not the seat.
- **THE REFINEMENT:** Fast Action Mode (SN-2954) said how the rounds move; this says what the speed is for — right first time.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: "Quicker is not better, right is right" (his charge, 2026-11-15 23:55Z) — and this is that charge as a standing order for today. The failure mode of fast action is obvious: many agents, each slightly misunderstanding, each building slightly wrong, all at once — and the captain spends the day redoing instead of delivering. The brief is the creation instrument: if it carries the whole understanding, the speed is safe; if it doesn't, the speed is the problem. Right first time is not a hope, it is the guard, enforced by the chain.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: The composer is where the river starts — every post on every feed begins there. If the composer is confusing (which feed? which kind of post? who sees it?), the feed fills with mistakes. If the composer is beautiful and obvious, the feed fills with beautiful posts. And the bar is not "does it work" — it is "is it the most beautiful post anyone has seen." A button you don't notice is a button that isn't there: he didn't notice the Private button, so the eye that explains private/public is not decoration, it is the fix. And the feed chooser at the top is the mistake prevented: posting to the wrong feed is the mistake the composer exists to stop.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine you're about to draw a beautiful picture to show all your friends! First you pick which wall to hang it on, then you pick what kind of picture it is, then you draw it — and you can even talk instead of drawing! You can add up to nine photos, all together like a block. You can see how it will look before you hang it up. And there's a little eye that tells you who can see it. Then — post it!

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: It's like this, love — when you make a post, it should be the most beautiful post anyone has seen. First you choose which feed it goes to, dear, then you pick what kind of post it is — and each kind tells you plainly what it is, so you never have to guess. You write your words — or speak them! — and you can add up to nine photos, all together. You see how it will look as you type, you pick when it goes out, and a little eye tells you who can see it. Then you post it. Lovely!

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: The composer, 10 out of 10: feed chooser at the top, each post type explained, name, words with speak, up to nine photos as a block with the size stated plainly, preview as you type, scheduler, private/public with an eye that explains, Post it. The post itself: the most beautiful post in the network.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- **FEED CHOOSER FIRST:** at the top, choose the feed you want to post to — a dropdown, your pick. Posting to the wrong feed is the mistake the composer prevents.
- **EACH TYPE EXPLAINED:** Make a post · Naya note · Smart note — three pills, and each one says what it IS, in plain words, right there.
- **NAME:** visitor or owner.
- **WORDS WITH SPEAK:** a big field, with the mic, so you can talk it instead of typing.
- **PHOTO — UP TO NINE, AS A BLOCK:** add a photo, keep going to nine, shown as a block. The composer SAYS what size photo you can upload, plainly, before you pick one. The size itself is his call.
- **PREVIEW AS YOU TYPE:** title, photo and words, exactly as they will post. What you see is what lands.
- **SCHEDULE:** the scheduler works — pick when it goes out.
- **PRIVATE/PUBLIC WITH AN EYE:** the choice is visible, not hidden: a little eye that explains who sees it, who doesn't. He didn't notice the Private button — a button you don't notice is a button that isn't there.
- **POST IT:** one button. Click, and it's on the feed.
- **OPEN QUESTION:** are the photos too big on a phone? His question, not a decision.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: The composer is judged by what lands on the feed, not by what the dialog looks like: if the post is the most beautiful post in the network, the composer did its job. Every element in the spec prevents a real mistake — the wrong feed, the wrong kind, the wrong audience, a photo size nobody stated — or explains something nobody understood. And the open question is the honesty: the photos are huge on his laptop, and he doesn't know if they're too big on a phone — so the round answers it by looking, not by guessing.

notes.title: The Full-Screen Law
notes.subtitle: Shawn, 2026-11-16 ~16:2xZ, dictation (the anatomy of a smart app), spoken over his screenshot of the "Your score — where every point came from" pop-up — a small panel, top-left, hard to read, with the "Open the ledger" link at its foot — THE FULL-SCREEN LAW. His words, verbatim: **"where it says open the ledger that looks terrible like this this presentation of the point system is very low level right so the nice one thing I want to say about when you have these pop-up screens you have the whole screen to work with you don't have to make them so small in fact I would encourage you to make them big or almost full screen so that the user gets this full screen experience regardless of the information on the screen right like why here I'll show you like this is how much of the screen you're showing and how look how hard it is to read it when it could just pop up full screen and have an X in the corner you exit out so we always give like max experience to the user does that make sense."** The law, as recorded in the anatomy v2 draft (§5), DRAFT — the official 2026-11-11 anatomy stands until he ratifies v2: **when a pop-up opens, you have the whole screen to work with. Use it.** Every pop-up — the score breakdown, the composer, every dialog, every detail view — opens big, almost full screen, with an X in the corner to exit. The user gets the full-screen experience regardless of what information is on the screen. Small pop-ups are done; the score breakdown and the composer are both too small today. **CORRECTION COMPOUND (same pass):** smart note (this note) + Factory/inventory update (THE-INVENTORY.md — the law entered as a rule) + brief-template update (DESIGN-BRIEF-TEMPLATE.md — every brief from today carries the law) + mail to the other Nayas + PI + GitHub. The full-screen round builds it (first of the four rounds after the anatomy: full-screen → composer → settings → stars; score breakdown first).

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: A pop-up that uses a corner of the screen wastes the screen and insults the citizen's eyes: tiny text, hard to read, while the rest of the screen sits empty and black. The whole screen is there — use it. Max experience is not a luxury for big screens; it is the standard for every screen, regardless of how much information is on it. "Regardless of the information on the screen" is the key: a pop-up with three lines deserves the full screen just as much as a pop-up with three hundred, because the citizen's eyes are the same size either way. A small pop-up is a fail, the same as a flat button.

The room is YOURS — open the present right in the middle, big and beautiful, so you can see everything! That's the law: pop-ups open big, almost the whole screen, with a little X to close them.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: It's like this, love — when a little window pops up, it shouldn't be a tiny thing squished in the corner that you can hardly read. You've got the whole screen, dear — use it! layers.name: Naya Note

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- **THE WHOLE SCREEN:** when a pop-up opens, you have the whole screen to work with. Use it.
- **BIG, ALMOST FULL SCREEN:** every pop-up — the score breakdown, the composer, every dialog, every detail view — opens big, almost full screen.
- **X IN THE CORNER:** an X in the corner to exit, always.
- **REGARDLESS OF THE INFORMATION:** the full-screen experience holds no matter how much — or how little — information is on the screen.
- **A FAIL, LIKE A FLAT BUTTON:** a small pop-up is a fail, the same as a flat button.
- **THE COMPOUND RAN:** smart note + inventory + brief-template + mail + PI + GitHub, same pass.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: The score pop-up in his screenshot is the proof: 5,480 points, every row traced, and it reads like a receipt taped to the corner of a billboard. The information is good — the presentation is low level. The law fixes the presentation everywhere at once, instead of fixing one pop-up at a time forever: any round that builds or touches a pop-up builds it full screen, and the checker can fail a small pop-up on sight. That is the Correction Compound working: one correction, in the note, the inventory, the template, the mail, PI, and GitHub — so the next builder cannot make the same mistake.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Points are authority — more points, more post weight — but a number alone tells the citizen nothing about where they stand. The level is the story of the number: what you are called, how far up the bar you are, what the next level gets you. The name changing with the level makes the progress visible in the one place the citizen always looks: under their own name. And the rewards, stated plainly, are what make the next level worth reaching for. Five stars, you're a five star member; ten stars, a ten star member — the name IS the level.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine you collect shiny stars, and every time you get enough points you earn a new star — up to ten stars! And your special name changes as you grow: when you have five stars you're a five star member, and when you have ten stars you're a ten star member! And there's a bar that shows how far up you've climbed, and if you tap it, you can see all the star names and what you get at each one!

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: It's like this, love — under your name there's a spot that says what level you're at, like a little badge that grows with you. When you reach five stars, you're a five star member, dear, and when you reach ten stars, you're a ten star member — your name changes all by itself! And there's a bar that goes all the way up to ten stars, and if you tap it, you can see all the levels, how the points work, and what you get at each one. Lovely, isn't it?

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: Under the profile, your level. The name changes with the level — five stars, five star member; ten stars, ten star member. A bar to ten stars; click to see every level, how points work, and what each level gets.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- **THE SPOT:** just underneath the profile, a spot says what level you're at.
- **THE NAME IS THE LEVEL:** the name changes automatically with the level — five stars, a five star member; ten stars, a ten star member.
- **THE BAR:** a bar runs all the way up to 10 stars, visible in the profile.
- **THE CLICK:** click it and you see your level, the names of all the different levels, how the points work, and what you actually get at each amount of points.
- **HIS CALL, NOT INVENTED:** the names of all ten levels and what each level gets — his words. His example: Sterling, or higher.
- **THE LEDGER:** every point traces to something you did; the score breakdown is presented beautifully, full screen (SN-2966).

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: A points number without a level is a scoreboard nobody reads; a level without rewards is a title nobody wants. Together they are the reason to come back: the name you carry, the bar you climb, the thing you get at the next step. And the boundary matters as much as the shape: the level names and rewards are his words, not ours — invented names would be our game, not his. The shape is locked (1–10 stars, name changes with level, bar to ten, click to see it all); the words wait on him.

Three is the number because three is a choice — one is a link, three is a top three, and a top three is a statement about who you are.

layers.name: What It Means

- **THE NUMBER IS THREE:** a top three, not a link farm.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: A page that only points inward is a dead end; a page that points outward to the citizen's own world is a doorway. The citizen's profiles elsewhere are part of who they are — the page should send visitors there, not hold them hostage. And the column being ours today is the mistake: it tells the visitor about us when it should be telling them about the citizen.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: This is the onboarding promise made visible: what you tell the system is how the system finds people like you. The more you tell it, the more it finds; if you don't set it, they can't find you; if you don't want to be found, don't set it. layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:

- **WHAT IT DOES:** people into those things show up in your feed as connections; content about those things shows up in your feed; people get recommended to you.

- **THE RULE:** if you don't set it, they can't find you. If you don't want to be found, don't set it.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: Auto-Match is only as good as what the citizen tells it — and a citizen who is asked everything at once, with no choice, tells it nothing. The menu with on/off switches is what makes the telling safe: each question is a separate, small, reversible choice. And the content-source setting is the same idea for the feed: the citizen chooses what the internet is for them, instead of the internet choosing for them. That is the customizable internet, and it only works if the citizen is the one customizing.

And where you are in the world: **"you can say they can say our network Ninet never shares your location okay this is solely to connect you with people that are like-minded so if you want to connect with people that are in Canada for example where I'm from you click you can click Canada if you want BC as well you can click BC if you want your town you can click your town."** Country, then region, then town — each level the citizen's choice, and the location is never shared: it exists solely to connect you with like-minded people. Recorded in the anatomy v2 draft (§3, Settings — public or private; demographics), DRAFT — the official 2026-11-11 anatomy stands until he ratifies v2. This sharpens the 2026-11-04 PRIVACY LAW (NayaNET is a private system; citizens use aliases) and the 2026-11-05 onboarding + auto-match decisions: location is a matching signal, never a shared fact.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Privacy is the promise the whole system stands on: NayaNET never shares your location, full stop. The location questions are not surveillance — they are the matching signal, and only the matching signal. The citizen tells the system where they are so it can find people like them, and the system never tells anyone else. Public or private is the same promise at the page level: the citizen chooses who the page is for. And the levels are the citizen's choice too — country, region, town, each one separately, because "Canada" and "my town" are very different amounts of trust.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine you get to choose: is your page open for everyone to see, or just for your friends? That's your choice! And where you live — that's a secret the system keeps just for finding friends like you. It never tells anyone where you are. Never ever!

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: It's like this, love — your page can be open to everyone or private, just for the people you choose. And where you live stays between you and the system, dear — it never tells a soul. It's only used to find lovely people near you who like the same things you do. Canada, or BC, or your town — you choose how much you say, and it stays private.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: Public or private — your choice, in Settings. Where you are is never shared: country, region, town, each your choice, solely to connect you with like-minded people.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- **PUBLIC OR PRIVATE:** the page can be public or private, the citizen's choice, in Settings.
- **LOCATION NEVER SHARED:** NayaNET never shares your location — full stop.
- **SOLELY TO CONNECT:** the location exists solely to connect you with people who are like-minded.
- **THE LEVELS ARE THE CHOICE:** country, then region, then town — each level the citizen's choice (Canada, then BC, then your town).
- **THE SHARPENING:** this is the 2026-11-04 Privacy Law and the 2026-11-05 auto-match decisions made concrete — location is a matching signal, never a shared fact.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: If the system shared location, the whole promise would break: citizens tell the system where they are because they trust it won't tell anyone. The moment that trust breaks, the demographics go unanswered, Auto-Match goes blind, and the feed stops finding people like you. "Never shares" has to be a law, not a setting — a setting can be toggled, a law cannot. And public-or-private is the same law at the page level: the citizen decides who the page is for, and the system obeys.

The orb library is the system showing off what it already has — every colour, every initial, for anyone or anything.

- **READ-IT-ALL IS FOR THE TEXT:** the text / letter may offer read-it-all-at-once. Text is read, not watched.
- **THE END BUTTONS:** bigger, clearer, more impressive presentation, so it is clear which one is which.
- **THE DECK IS A DECK:** the slideshow ends at the last image and never continues sideways into the scroll-down agreement (the standing Visual Collective Agreement rule).

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: A show-all option on the visual would be the easiest button in the world to add — and it would quietly destroy the deck. The discipline is in refusing it: the deck's power is the unfolding, and the unfolding only exists one slide at a time. The text/video split is the principle: give the citizen the whole thing where the whole thing is the experience (text), and never where the sequence IS the experience (video).

Going back and forth simply is not a convenience — it is the system working. The back button is the citizen's freedom to change their mind, and it costs nothing: elegant, beautiful, clean, blocking nothing. "Most of the pages" is his honesty — a page that truly has nowhere to go back to doesn't need one — but the default is that it is there, and a view you entered is a view you can leave.

layers.name: Naya Note

layers.name: What It Means

layers.name: Why It Matters

The back button is the cheapest freedom in the system — one control, always in the same spirit — and it is what makes trying things safe. A citizen who can always go back will always try the next thing; a citizen who got stuck once will hesitate forever.

notes.title: Fast Action Mode
notes.subtitle: Shawn, 2026-11-16 16:01Z — his name for it: "the fast action plan". FAST ACTION MODE: the mode is continuous back-and-forth, not send-it-away. He says something, it gets done right away and comes back right away; he makes another edit, it comes back right away. NOT send-it-away-and-see-it-hours-later-or-the-next-day — that doesn't work for him, it's exhausting. The difference: send-off mode is the seat relay (maker → checker → captain) with each step queued, and delivery held until a whole chain finishes or bundled with another round — that is what made the visual agreement sit 10 hours and the sidebar round take hours. Fast action mode: build a piece, verify it myself right away, show it to him the same pass, he reacts, fix, back again. Nothing sits. Nothing held for another round. The relay still verifies (maker → checker → captain's eye), but the captain's eye and the delivery happen the same pass the report lands — no holding, no bundling. Recorded in AGENTS.md + MEMORY.md the same minute (the AGENTS.md entry and the MEMORY.md entry carry the same text); this note files the lesson so the mode survives the message. This supersedes the send-off shape wherever the relay was holding delivery for a chain or bundling it with another round — it does not supersede the relay itself, the Self-Check Law, or the protected gates.

Every hold is a decision the machine made for him without asking: "this can wait." Fast action takes that decision back: nothing can wait, because waiting is what exhausts him. The test of the mode is the clock between his word and his screen — minutes, not hours — and the proof is the same pass, not the next round.

A project is not a fourth thing and not a separate concept — a business can be a project, a thing can be a project, a project can be its own feed, because a project IS a world you add, and a world's feed is a feed. And the one row is the discipline: kinds first (All / Smart Notes / Naya Notes / Posts), then topics, one row, never two — two rows is how the "All" filter became a second control and the glow became a defect.

Nothing else fits in the box — if it's not one of those three, it doesn't go in! And a project? A project is just a world you add — like adding a new room to your house, and that room has its own feed box! And the little filter buttons sit in ONE neat row: first the kinds (All, Smart Notes, Naya Notes, Posts), then the topics. One row, nice and tidy!

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: It's like this, love — your feed is a tidy little shelf that holds exactly three things: Naya's notes, smart notes, and posts. Nothing else goes on that shelf — if it's not one of those three, it lives somewhere else. And a project? A project is just a world you add, dear — like adding a new room to the house, and that room has its own shelf. The little filter buttons sit in one neat row: first the kinds, then the subjects. layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: A feed is three things: Naya Notes, Smart Notes, posts. Nothing else. A project is a world you add. One filter row: kinds first, then topics. The note lives where the work is.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- **THE THREE THINGS:** a feed consists of exactly Naya Notes, Smart Notes, and posts. Nothing else. Anything that is none of the three does not belong on a feed.
- **THE NOTE LIVES WHERE THE WORK IS:** Naya makes notes for you on the feed; if that feed is shared with someone on your team, they see the note on that feed.
- **A FEED CAN BE A PROJECT:** a business can be a project, a thing can be a project, or a project can be its own separate feed — a project IS a world you add. No separate project-feed concept.
- **THE FILTERS:** Smart Tabs are the filters; the point is a super-organized system — the smartest, most intelligent way to keep things in line, organized, and findable. Show only Smart Notes / only Naya Notes / only posts.
- **ONE ROW, NOT TWO:** under the tabs, one chip row starting with the type chips All / Smart Notes / Naya Notes / Posts, then the topic chips. The existing "All" filter is the first chip of that row, not a separate control.
- **ACTIONS ARE NOT CONTENT:** the composer's Message / Mail / Create world are actions, not feed content.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: Without the law, every new card type finds its way onto the feed and the feed stops being a feed — it becomes a drawer. Three things is a test any builder can run in a glance: is this a Naya Note, a Smart Note, or a post? If not, it does not go on the feed. The project clause kills a whole category of future work: no separate project-feed system to build, no second feed concept to maintain — a project is a world, a world has a feed, done. And the one row kills the second-control defect at the root: "All" was a filter pretending to be a tab, and the glow was the symptom. One row, kinds first, topics after — the shape is the law made visible.

notes.title: Workers Paid Is Live
notes.subtitle: Shawn, 2026-11-16 15:39Z: he completed the Cloudflare Workers Paid purchase himself in the Cloudflare dashboard and sent the screenshot showing the subscription active — Workers Paid, $5/month, on the NayaPOWER account. He asked whether he needs to store something in Cloudflare secure, thinking it auto-upgraded. The captain's answer: nothing to store — he is right, it is automatic. The upgrade applies account-wide; the existing API token/connection is unchanged, so there is nothing new to save anywhere. Effect: the KV free quota wall from earlier today is gone — KV writes go from 1,000/day to 1M/month (also 500 workers per account, up from 100). This unblocks the walk completion, the thank-you loop, and the intelligence-room updates that were failing on quota — all four PI state-publish runs in the 14:00–15:00Z hour had failed HTTP 429, the sixteenth consecutive hour of the wall, with the intelligence room's state.json stale. The captain verified at ~15:40Z with a live KV write via the registered Cloudflare connection (PUT returned success) and cleaned the test key up (DELETE returned success). The two midnight crons waiting on the quota reset — `handoff-reproof-after-kv-reset` (was 2026-11-17 00:30Z) and `thankyou-resume-after-kv-reset` (was 2026-11-17 00:45Z) — were run early instead and paused so they do not double-fire; at flush their early runs were queued/pending, NOT recorded as completed or verified. notes.title: Verify by Blob, Never by cb
notes.subtitle: Method caveat, recorded honestly in the My World redesign delivery, 2026-11-16 10:07Z (staged Personal sha 9b4353d8, 3,121,411 B, branch personal/my-world-redesign-20261116, commit 7c9e3c83, blob 2dd70c7e): the proof host IGNORES `cb` — curling an old build's URL with a new/old `cb` returns the current build. Old builds must be verified from the branch's own blob (GitHub blob API decode) or an independently curled copy, never by a cb URL. The captain's own verification before delivery did it right: curl of the staged URL byte-identical (3,121,411 B, sha 9b4353d8…, 0× nayanet.live) + own Firefox probe on her own curled copy, seeded citizen stores, real clicks. The same discipline runs through the day's other verdicts: the certificate round-4 captain re-curled all three staged shas (matched); the Hub alignment captain re-curled the staged Hub (200, sha matched); the about-unfold captain curl-verified the staged bytes (sha ba8fa387, 3,109,527 B, nayanet.live 0×).

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: A cache-buster that doesn't bust the cache is worse than no cache-buster at all — it tells you the build is verified while showing you a different build. The `cb` parameter looks like proof: same URL, different `cb`, surely a different build. It isn't. The proof host serves the current build whatever `cb` you pass, so a "verification" by cb URL can pass on bytes you never built and fail on bytes you did. The fix is to verify from the source of truth: the branch's own blob, decoded through the GitHub blob API, byte-compared to what you curled — or an independently curled copy you control. Every captain's-eye verification in the day's log does it this way, and that is why their deliveries hold.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine you have a magic box that always gives you the NEWEST toy, no matter which number you ask for! If you ask for toy number 5, you get the newest toy. If you ask for toy number 9, you still get the newest toy! So the number doesn't prove anything. To really check a toy, you have to look at the toy itself — not the number you asked for.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: It's like this, love — if the shop always hands you the latest loaf no matter which one you point at, then pointing doesn't tell you which loaf you got. You have to look at the loaf itself. Same here: the little `cb` number doesn't change what comes back, so you check the real thing — the blob — not the number.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: Verify by blob, never by cb. The proof host ignores `cb` — a cb URL can pass on bytes you never built.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- **THE FACT:** the proof host IGNORES `cb` — curling an old build's URL with a new/old `cb` returns the current build.
- **THE RULE:** old builds are verified from the branch's own blob (GitHub blob API decode) or an independently curled copy — never by a cb URL.
- **THE PATTERN:** every captain's-eye verification in the day does it this way — re-curl the staged shas, byte-compare, probe your own curled copy.
- **THE RISK:** a cb "verification" can pass on bytes you never built — it looks like proof and proves nothing.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: Verification is the whole job — the loop's proof standard is "never claim done without proof", and a proof that proves the wrong build is worse than no proof, because it closes the item on false evidence. The My World delivery recorded the caveat honestly instead of burying it, and the fix is mechanical: blob API, byte compare, every time. A seat that learns this never wastes a round arguing with a "verified" build that was never the build under test.

notes.title: A Firefox Empty List Is a Probe Failure
notes.subtitle: Proven 2026-11-16, Connections eye (captain's own probe): Firefox in this VM loaded the staged page, loaded supabase-js, threw 0 page errors — and issued ZERO Supabase requests in a 90s poll, leaving the Connections list empty (0 tiles). The identical bytes in Chromium (via the h1-proxy-forwarder.py on 127.0.0.1:18080) fired the reads (invites, smart_mail_threads, smart_notes all 200) and rendered 3 tiles. Rule: any eye probe on a Supabase-fed section runs in Chromium through the forwarder; a Firefox empty-list result is a PROBE failure, never a page failure. Firefox remains fine for static sections (skills, my-world, about — where no live read gates the content). Written to ~/TOOLS.md the same pass. The forwarder: ~/workspace/project-intelligence/proof/pi-h1-evidence/h1-proxy-forwarder.py (stdlib only; handles CONNECT + plain HTTP; credentials from https_proxy in the environment at runtime, never written to disk) — start with nohup, point Chromium at http://127.0.0.1:18080, kill it when the probe is done. Related tool lesson re-confirmed this pass: `pkill -f <pattern>` SIGTERMs the exec shell itself when the pattern appears in its own command line — kill by PID from a bracket-trick grep instead.

The identical bytes in Chromium (via the h1-proxy-forwarder.py on 127.0.0.1:18080) fired the reads (invites, smart_mail_threads, smart_notes all 200) and rendered 3 tiles. Related tool lesson re-confirmed this pass: `pkill -f <pattern>` SIGTERMs the exec shell itself when the pattern appears in its own command line — kill by PID from a bracket-trick grep instead.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: The trap is a silent one: Firefox did everything right — page loaded, library loaded, zero errors — and still never asked Supabase for anything. A checker who trusts that silence will report "the list is empty" as a page failure, and a maker will chase a bug that doesn't exist, or worse, "fix" a working page. The proof is the control: identical bytes, different browser, reads fire, tiles render. So the rule is not a preference — it is a validity condition. Any eye probe on a Supabase-fed section that runs in VM Firefox and finds an empty list has proven nothing about the page; it has proven something about the probe. Chromium through the forwarder is the instrument for live reads; Firefox is the instrument for static sections. And the forwarder itself is the other half of the lesson: Chromium can't reach the network directly here (the egress proxy drops unauthenticated requests without a 407, and Chromium never sends preemptive Proxy-Authorization — Firefox does, which is why Firefox works unaided) — so the localhost forwarder adds the header at runtime, never from disk.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine you ask your friend to fetch you some apples, and your friend walks to the shop, stands outside, and never goes in — and comes back with no apples! Did the shop have no apples? No! Your friend just never asked! That's Firefox with the Supabase shop. Chromium is the friend who actually walks in and asks — and comes back with apples.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: It's like this, love — if you send someone to the market and they come back empty-handed, you check whether they actually went in before you blame the market. Firefox walks to the door and never goes in — no errors, no fuss, just empty hands. Chromium walks in and asks, and comes back with the goods. So when the list is empty, you ask which friend you sent.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: A Firefox empty list is a probe failure, never a page failure. Supabase-fed eye probes run in Chromium through the forwarder.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- **THE FACT:** VM Firefox loads the page and supabase-js, throws 0 errors, and issues ZERO Supabase requests in 90s — the list stays empty.
- **THE CONTROL:** identical bytes in Chromium (via the forwarder) fire the reads (invites, smart_mail_threads, smart_notes all 200) and render the tiles.
- **THE RULE:** any eye probe on a Supabase-fed section runs in Chromium through the forwarder; a Firefox empty-list result is a PROBE failure, never a page failure.
- **THE SCOPE:** Firefox remains fine for static sections — skills, my-world, about — where no live read gates the content.
- **THE INSTRUMENT:** h1-proxy-forwarder.py on 127.0.0.1:18080 — credentials from the environment at runtime, never written to disk; kill it when the probe is done.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: A false failure is worse than a missed failure: it sends a maker to fix a working page, burns a round, and teaches the team to distrust a page that was fine. The Connections round could have gone exactly that way — the list was empty in Firefox, the page was innocent. The rule protects the verdict: a probe that cannot see the data cannot judge the page. It also protects the next Naya, who will otherwise rediscover this silence the expensive way.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: This is the third time the same pattern has bitten: agent-dir mtime quiet ≠ dead. The about-unfold lane at 08:00Z (coordinator quiet ~22 min, maker child active 6 seconds ago — alive, no poke), the my-world lane at 09:19Z and 09:47Z (coordinator quiet while the maker was active seconds ago — alive, no poke), and now the sidebar lane at 13:20Z — where the lesson was NOT applied and the close went through. The coordinator was waiting on its maker child, exactly as a coordinator should; its own dir had nothing new to write. Closing it killed the maker mid-work and lost ~11 minutes plus the blob-verification progress. The fix is mechanical, not a judgment call: before any close-or-declare-dead, run subagent.list with scope descendants and look at the children. If a child is running, the lane is alive. The captain's correction of the board is the other half: a false declaration does not stand — it is replaced, in writing, with what actually happened.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine a teacher waiting quietly while her student does the work — the teacher isn't asleep, she's WAITING! If you send the teacher home because she's quiet, the student stops working too, and all their work is lost! So before you ever send anyone home, you check: is their student still working? If yes — the lane is ALIVE. Quiet does not mean dead!

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: It's like this, love — a mother hen sitting quiet on the nest isn't doing nothing, she's keeping the eggs warm. You don't chase her off because she's still. You look underneath first: if the chicks are there and warm, she's working. Same with these seats — check the children before you close the parent, or you lose the whole nest.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: Check the descendants before you close. Dir mtime quiet is not dead — the maker child is the activity signal. A close kills its children.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
- **THE RULE:** never declare a coordinator dead or close it without a descendants-scope subagent.list check first.
- **THE SIGNAL:** agent-dir mtime quiet ≠ dead — the maker child running is the activity signal; a coordinator waiting on its maker is normal.
- **THE COST:** a close cascades and CANCELS the maker mid-work — this time ~11 min lost, blob-verification progress gone.
- **THE PROOF:** sidebar coordinator d8cf8c4f was ALIVE at close — blob checks PASSED, H1 written, maker 343f1acf running 675s; its completion report landed 13:23:24Z, seconds after the close.
- **THE CORRECTION:** the false "dead" declaration was replaced on THE-FLOOR.md with a 13:25Z CORRECTION entry — a false declaration does not stand.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: The machine's worst failure mode is not a seat going quiet — it is the captain killing a live seat by mistake. Every close is irreversible for the work in flight: the maker dies with the coordinator, the progress dies with the maker, and the replacement starts from zero. The descendants check costs seconds and prevents exactly that. It is already the proven pattern from 08:00Z and 09:19Z — the lesson this time is that a pattern proven twice and not applied the third time is a lesson not yet learned, and now it is law in AGENTS.md so the fourth time never happens.

notes.title: The Free Tier Wall — Count Your Writes
notes.subtitle: Shawn's night, 2026-11-16 06:15–06:26Z. The captain's own eye walks (fresh citizens capteye1 at 390, capteye2 at 1851×1009, capteye3 at 390 on retry) ALL failed at the building step — "Something went wrong building your world." with a "Try again" button; Try again also failed. The retry used the fix checker's EXACT answers and still failed — answer content ruled out. Console: 0 errors — the page catches the failed completion call and shows the error screen silently. Root cause pinned by the captain's own curls: POST /api/welcome/complete = HTTP 500, Cloudflare error 1101 (worker threw) — twice, minimal payload and complete UI-shaped payload. The endpoint WORKED minutes earlier: the fix checker's five walks built fine 05:51–06:03Z. The break arrived AFTER ~06:03Z, on unchanged page bytes — no new citizen could complete the walk. Endpoint-fix coordinator f96aab13 COMPLETED 06:24:59Z. Root cause proven, not guessed: the account hit Cloudflare KV's Workers Free daily write limit (1,000 writes/day, account-wide). The complete handler's first unguarded `WELCOME_ASSETS.put` threw → worker 1101. Deployed bytes were the unchanged 05:50:27Z deploy; binding present and correct — NOT the Nov 14 wipe, NOT a code change, NOT Supabase (handler run locally in Node with stub KV returned HTTP 200 with pages; Supabase behaves as designed — projects insert succeeds, citizen_worlds/page_about 401 RLS → kv-fallback). A throw-capturing probe worker caught the exact throw: "KV put() limit exceeded for the day." Cloudflare KV API independently confirmed: direct write → HTTP 429, error 10048. Quota resets 00:00 UTC. This worker does 5 puts per completion, so ~200 test completions across all seats today exhausted it — it broke right after the checker's 06:03Z walks.
