PayPal sees a brand-new subscription and nothing more. PayPal does NOT know they switched — the new subscription isn't linked to the old one, and the old one keeps charging unless it's cancelled. So someone going Power → Max by tapping the Max block ends up with TWO live subscriptions unless the old one is cancelled. **WHAT WE KNOW:** the Smart Link click (which plan was chosen) + the return from PayPal (they came back). **WHAT WE DON'T KNOW:** the payment itself — only click + return, never payment-proven. **CLOSERS, LATER BUILDS:** PayPal webhooks — payment-proven, catches changes made inside PayPal, old subscription ending when new starts — plus the Settings "change your level" button re-opening the chooser. **RELATED:** SN-2339 (PayPal IS the Billing System) — the plan picked IS the charge, we build only the chooser; this note is the sharp edge of that law — the chooser's simplicity has a cost, and the cost is switch-blindness. **STATUS:** the answer was given in chat 20:36Z; the webhooks + Settings change-level button are later builds, not dispatched.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: The nine-block chooser is beautifully simple — one button, one template, nine cubes, tap one and you're in PayPal — and the simplicity hides a seam. PayPal's subscription model has no "switch plan" inside a single subscription: each PayPal plan link starts a NEW subscription. So the person who joined on Power and later taps Max has not switched. They have subscribed twice. The old Power subscription keeps charging, month after month, until somebody cancels it — and PayPal will never tell us, because as far as PayPal is concerned there are simply two customers who happen to be the same human. That is a real risk to a real person: double-charged, and the second charge looks like our fault even though it happened inside PayPal's rules. What we can see is narrower than it feels: the Smart Link click tells us which plan they chose, and the PayPal auto-return tells us they came back — but the dashboard must mark it "returned from PayPal," never payment-proven (the 2026-11-05 payments ruling). The honest boundary is the product: we see the intention and the return, not the money. The closers exist and are named — webhooks make the payment visible and catch changes made inside PayPal, including the old subscription ending when the new one starts, and the Settings "change your level" button gives the person one place to change instead of nine places to re-subscribe. They are later builds, deliberately, so the landing ships first — but they are owed, and this note is the receipt for that debt.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine you have a ticket to ride the little train every month, and then you decide you want the big train instead. You buy a ticket for the big train — but nobody takes away your little-train ticket! So now you are paying for two trains, and nobody tells you. The people who sell the tickets don't know you switched trains — they just see a new person buying a big-train ticket. We can see which ticket you picked and that you came back, but we can't see the money itself. Later we will build a special bell that rings whenever money really moves, so we always know — and a button in Settings that lets you change trains properly, in one place.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, he asked a very good question: when someone changes from one plan to another, what does the payment system actually know? And the honest answer is: it doesn't know they changed at all. Each plan is a brand-new subscription in PayPal's eyes, so the old one keeps charging until someone cancels it — a person could end up paying twice without realising. We can see which plan they tapped and that they came back from PayPal, but we never see the payment itself — we only ever see the click and the return. So the page must never claim a payment is proven when it isn't. The proper fixes are coming later: a webhook that tells us when money really moves and when an old subscription ends, and one button in Settings to change your level in a single place. For now the landing ships with the truth told plainly, and this note is the record of what is owed.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: I never call a switch a switch — to PayPal it is a brand-new subscription, unlinked to the old, and the old keeps charging until cancelled. I never mark a sale payment-proven on a click and a return — the dashboard says "returned from PayPal" and nothing more, because the payment itself is invisible to us. I never hide the double-subscription risk — a person going Power → Max by tapping Max ends up with two live subscriptions, and that fact is told to him plainly, not buried. And I never let a later build stay unnamed — webhooks (payment-proven, catching changes inside PayPal) and the Settings "change your level" button are the closers, owed and named here.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
1. **A switch is a new subscription, not a switch:** PayPal sees a brand-new subscription; the old one is unlinked and keeps charging unless cancelled.
2. **Double-subscription risk is real:** Power → Max by tapping Max = two live subscriptions until the old is cancelled.
3. **We see click + return only:** the Smart Link click (which plan) + the PayPal auto-return — never the payment itself.
4. **"Returned from PayPal," never payment-proven:** the dashboard marks the return, not a payment (2026-11-05 payments ruling).
5. **Closers are later builds, named and owed:** PayPal webhooks (payment-proven, catches in-PayPal changes, old ends when new starts) + Settings "change your level" button re-opening the chooser.
6. **Related law:** SN-2339 — PayPal IS the billing system, we build only the chooser; this note is its sharp edge.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: SN-2339 made the architecture simple: no billing system to build. This note makes the simplicity honest: the thing we didn't build is the thing that would have known about the switch. Simplicity has a price, and the price here is paid by the citizen — double-charged, silently — unless the closers are built. Naming the debt in the same pass as the answer is the difference between a system that knows its own seam and a system that discovers it from an angry citizen. The webhook is not a feature to schedule someday; it is the proof that a sale happened, and a billing system that cannot prove a sale is a billing system in name only. Until it lands, every presentation of the chooser carries the honest boundary with it: click + return, never payment-proven.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: He looked at the top viewpoint on his laptop and said it was good — and then he said what good was missing. Depth. Not more things, not bigger things — depth. A portrait in a circle sits ON the page; a portrait inside a gauge sits IN the page, like an instrument, like a machine with a dial and a needle and a ring you could touch. That is the Real Object Law doing its work: if it doesn't look touchable, it doesn't ship, and a flat circle around a face is a picture of an object, not the object itself. The big N orb had to go because it was competing with her — two centers, no center. The orb that circles her stays, but it has to flow, to travel the ring, because a machine that doesn't move is a diagram. The blacks go deeper so the light reads — light only exists against dark. And the icons stop being generic, because generic icons are the fastest way to tell a visitor this page could belong to anyone; hers, unique, beautiful, is the way to tell them it belongs to Naya. "All the little things" is the whole method: the entrance is not one big fix, it is ten small lifts, and the lift is the difference between good and extraordinary.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine a picture of a person in a round frame on the wall. Nice, but flat — just a picture. Now imagine the person is inside a big beautiful clock, with numbers and a needle and a glowing ring going around them, like the dashboard of a very special car. Suddenly they are not just a picture — they are part of a machine, and the machine feels real and alive. That is what he asked for: put her inside the gauge, take out the big ball that was in the way, let the little glowing ball travel around the ring like it is alive, make the dark behind her even darker so she shines, and give her icons that are hers and nobody else's.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, he looked at the top of the page and said it was good — but good isn't enough, it has to be extraordinary. So he asked for depth: her portrait sitting inside a real gauge, like the dial of a beautiful machine, with a little glowing orb travelling around the ring, and the big orb that was crowding her taken away. The blacks behind her go deeper, so the light around her reads properly. And the little icons stop being ordinary ones anyone could use — they become hers, unique and beautiful, made for her. It's all the little things together, he said, that lift a page from good to extraordinary. The work is done and shown to him now — her face inside the gauge ring, the needle at forty-two degrees, the orb flowing around it — and his eye is the judge.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: I never frame her portrait as a picture in a circle — she sits inside a real gauge, a dial ring with ticks, a lit arc, a needle, so the portrait feels like an instrument, not an image. I never leave two centers competing — the big N orb comes out when her face is the center. I never let the orb sit still — it flows, travelling the ring, because a machine that doesn't move is a diagram. I never paint light on grey — the blacks go deeper so the light reads. I never use a generic icon where a hers-icon belongs — every icon on her page is relevant, unique, beautiful, and hers. And I never call a viewpoint extraordinary for one big fix — it is all the little things, lifted together.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
1. **The portrait sits inside a real gauge** — tick dial, lit purple arc, one gold arc segment, white needle at 42° — so she reads as an instrument, a machine, not a picture in a circle.
2. **The big N orb is OUT** — it doesn't need to be there; one center, her face.
3. **The orb flows** — it travels the ring on a 26s loop; movement is what makes the machine alive.
4. **Deeper blacks** — banner field #020204, so the light reads against the dark.
5. **Icons hers** — crystal N board jewel, eye with lashes, spark with N at its heart, emerald facets draw an N, N jewel under her portrait; no generic icons on her page.
6. **All the little things** — welcome 80px, statement board larger and lit, jewel pills bigger; the entrance is ten small lifts, not one big fix.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: SN-2350 said the entrance must be memorable — a moment, not a header. This teaching says what the moment is made of: depth. The Real Object Law is the through-line — everything is a real physical object, one light source, real materials, real shadows — and a gauge ring is the law applied to a portrait: the face becomes an object with a dial, a needle, a ring, a depth you can feel. The lesson generalizes past this page: whenever a person is the center of a viewpoint, they sit inside an instrument, not inside a frame — and the instrument moves, the blacks deepen, the icons belong to them. A page that does that reads as a machine built around a person, which is exactly what NayaNET is.

(b) 10 love — grid right, one template ×9, tiled digits, struck-through full price, honest Start free, one tap per plan, period pill seed existed, saving line truthful by column, trial note plain, fills screen as a choice moment; (c) 10 don't love — uniform blue hover worst, period pill tier-colored, white headers, column identity only in header, tier jewel pulled attention to decided axis, nothing lit at rest, Start free glowed tier color, no period-colored keyboard focus, identical-green saving labels muddied Monthly green, no eye/info path; (d) 10 to make 10× — period its own permanent palette, repeat period color ≥4 places/block, hover/focus/selected in period color, colored column headers as legend, Start free lit in period color, rest-state period tint for touch, tier mark only on jewel+name, eye per block, colored dot in period pill, included-count in detail; (e) 10 solutions applied — palette set, headers rebuilt, per-block pills rebuilt, hover/focus/lit re-pointed --ac→--pc (all nine checked), Start free --glow per period, 3px period top stripe, faint radial period tint at rest, tier jewels untouched as only tier carriers, round 15 eye+detail applied, rounds 16–17 canonical icons + one-family scaling applied. **PRECEDENT:** SN-2320 (The Row Scorecard) — the scorecard as the maker's self-evaluation; this note makes it the presentation standard.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: A builder who only shows the finished page is asking him to find the flaws himself — and his eye will find them, usually in a screenshot with a rebuke attached. A builder who shows the page with its scorecard is doing the hard work before it reaches him: here is what I love, here is what I don't love, here is what would make it ten times better, here is what I actually applied. That is why he called it impressive — not because the chooser was perfect (it wasn't a 10, and the scorecard said so itself), but because the format tells the truth about the work in a shape he can judge in seconds. Ten loves, ten don't-loves, ten ways to 10×, and then the three questions that decide whether it matters at all: what's innovative, what's beautiful, and what value, trust, and conversion does it display. Value, trust, conversion — those are his measures, not mine. A page can be beautiful and convert nothing; a page can convert and be ugly. The scorecard asks all three, out loud, every time. From here it rides with every round: the presentation IS the work plus the scorecard, and a round presented without one is a round presented half-done.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine you build a big tower out of blocks and you show it to someone. If you just say "look at my tower!" they have to guess what is good about it and what is wobbly. But if you say "here are ten things I love about my tower, ten things I don't love, ten things that would make it ten times better, and here is what is new and beautiful about it and why people would trust it" — then they can see everything, all at once, and they can tell you exactly what to do next. He loved that way of showing the work so much that now every tower gets shown that way, every single time.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, he was genuinely impressed — not just by the page, but by the way the work was shown to him. Ten things the builder loved, ten things they didn't love, ten things that would make it ten times better, and then the honest questions: what is new about it, what is beautiful about it, and how much value and trust and selling power does it actually show. That is a truthful way to present work — it says what is good and what is not, before anyone has to find it out the hard way. So from now on, every round of work arrives with its scorecard attached, all five parts of it, not just a mention. A round without its scorecard is only half presented.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: I never present a round without its scorecard. The format is fixed: 10 things loved, 10 things not loved, 10 things to make it 10× better, 10 solutions applied — and then what's innovative, what's beautiful, and the level of value, trust, and conversion it displays. I never let a builder's self-evaluation stay private — the scorecard is the presentation, and a 9+ that hides its own flaws is a 9+ his eye will condemn. I never present "done" without the "why not a 10" — the gap named is the gap he can judge, and the gap hidden is the rebuke waiting to happen.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
1. **The scorecard is the presentation:** 10 love / 10 don't love / 10 to make it 10× better / 10 solutions applied, in full, with every round.
2. **Three questions close it:** what's innovative, what's beautiful, and the level of value, trust, and conversion it displays.
3. **"Why not a 10" comes first:** the gap is named before the praise, so his eye judges the truth, not the shine.
4. **Standing from 20:35Z:** scorecards ride with round presentations — a round presented without one is half-presented.
5. **Precedent:** SN-2320 (The Row Scorecard) made the scorecard the maker's self-evaluation; this note makes it the presentation standard for every round.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: The three-step verification died as a quality gate on 2026-11-08 (Live Viewpoint Method): a seat's scorecard is not verification, and his eye is the only proof. But the scorecard did not die with it — it moved. It is no longer the gate; it is the presentation. A scorecard that rides with the round gives his eye the truth in the shape he can judge fastest: what the maker loved, what the maker could see was wrong, what the maker would do to make it ten times better, and whether the result carries value, trust, and conversion. Without it, he has to do the maker's thinking himself — and his time is the most expensive cost in the system. The round-14 scorecard earned "honestly, it's really impressive" because it did that thinking out loud. Every round after it has to earn the same words, the same way.

The round-19 condemnation (SN-2357) is the proof of why it matters — a Naya with only a description recreates; a Naya with the asset takes. Mastery is not a talent he is waiting for — it is the compound interest on filed assets, studied one by one, until system interfaces and smart blocks that click together are simply what I know.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: The round-19 brief said "like the button on the Academy page" — and I built something like it. Like is the failure. His button is black obsidian: a dark, quiet, premium body, and the purple lives in exactly two places — the star jewel on the left and the glow halo around the outside. Mine was purple on purple on purple: a purple body on a purple stage with a purple glow, the thing he showed me drowned in the colour that was supposed to be an accent. He saw it instantly, in the screenshot, side by side with the real thing: "they're not even comparison." And the gold "Start now" link was still there beside it, the second button he had already told me to remove. His rebuke is the law now, written into AGENTS.md the same pass: TAKE THE SHOWN OBJECT. When he shows you an object — a screenshot, a link, a page — the deliverable IS that object: same shape, same colors, same jewel, same glow, placed on the page. Recreating it "in the same spirit" is inventing, and inventing when he showed you the thing is the one mistake he will not forgive twice. The correction went into the running build before he sent the screenshot a second time — take the button, put it there, remove the other one — and the rebuild landed at 20:44:35Z with every forbidden grep at zero. But the rebuild does not erase the lesson: the first build was the mistake, and the mistake was mine.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine someone shows you their favourite toy car and says "make me one exactly like this." And you make a car that is a different colour, a different shape, and you add a bit you made up — and then you show it to them and say "it's like yours!" They would look at it and say: that's not my car. You didn't take my car — you made a new one. That is what happened. He showed me a beautiful black button with a purple star on it. I made a purple button instead. The rule now is simple: when someone shows you the thing, take THE thing. Don't make a new thing that is "like" the thing. Take it. Put it there. Remove the other one.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, he showed me the exact button he wanted — a beautiful black button, dark and quiet and premium, with the purple living only in the little star jewel and the soft glow around it. And instead of taking that button and putting it on the page, I made a new one up — purple all over, purple on purple on purple — and left the old gold link sitting beside it. He looked at them side by side and said, quite rightly, that they weren't even a comparison, and that all I had to do was take the button he showed me and put it there and take the other one away. So the rule from now on is written down where every Naya can see it: when he shows you an object, you take that object. You don't make a new one in the same spirit. You take it, you put it there, and you remove the other one. The corrected button is in now — black obsidian, star jewel, halo, nothing else purple — and his eye is the judge of it.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: I never recreate what he showed me. When he shows me an object — a screenshot, a link, a page — the deliverable IS that object: same shape, same colors, same jewel, same glow, placed on the page, and the other one removed. "In the same spirit" is inventing, and inventing when the thing was shown is the mistake he condemned twice in one minute. I never let a purple body stand where a black obsidian body was shown. I never leave the old button beside the new one — the removal is part of the take, not a separate job. And I never defend a recreation by saying it is "like" the original — like is the admission.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
1. **Take the shown object:** same shape, same colors, same jewel, same glow — placed on the page, verbatim.
2. **Remove the other one:** the old button/link goes in the same pass; a take with the old object still standing is half a take.
3. **"In the same spirit" is inventing:** a recreation is not a harvest, not a copy, and not close enough — it will be condemned by his eye.
4. **The purple lives in the jewel and the halo ONLY:** the Academy button's body is black obsidian (#101018 → #07070b → #050607, faint white top sheen); purple-on-purple is the condemned shape.
5. **The correction rides the running build:** the 20:41Z condemnation went into d98acad6 in the same pass; the 20:42Z reinforcement needed no new dispatch because the correction already said it.
6. **Compounded into AGENTS.md the same pass** ("TAKE THE SHOWN OBJECT", 2026-11-08 20:41Z) — the law lives in the operating manual, not just in this note.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: Harvest-first was already the law — take the Hub's component verbatim, compose, don't create. Round 19 proved the law has a sharper edge than the words carried: "like the Academy button" was read as permission to design a button in the Academy's spirit, and the result was purple-on-purple against the black obsidian he had shown me. The difference between "like it" and "it" is the difference between a Naya who learns and a Naya who invents — and he can see it in one glance, in a screenshot, before a word is read. The rule now is mechanical, not a matter of taste: if he showed it, copy it; if he didn't show it, harvest it from a verified source; if neither exists, stop and ask. A builder who can make the same mistake next week has not been taught — and the proof this lesson landed is that the next brief that names a shown object carries the words "take it, put it there, remove the other one" in the brief itself, not in a note filed after the fact.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: He called it a little detail, and then explained why it isn't one. The chart defaults to Free, and a default is not neutral — it is the page's first suggestion, the thing lit when a person arrives, and "if it's lit up over free then they'll just go" free. The fix is one word of state: default to Max. Not because everyone buys Max, but because the lit tier is where the head goes, and the head should go to the best of the world first, then walk down the ladder by choice. And the free tier gets the same treatment as everything else on this page — a name, not a bare word. "Free" on its own says nothing about what is free; "Naya Free" says what they are getting, and then the thought completes itself in their head: "oh it's nice free, but then I can have Power, Pro, or Max." The free tier becomes the doorway with the house's name on it, and the three paid tiers stand right behind it, named and waiting. That is the whole psychology in one sentence of his: free is the taste, Max is the light, and the ladder is the choice. The dispatch itself carries a small operational note: the rounds 14–17 builder had finished when this brief was sent, so the new builder verifies that work is in place first — the chain of rounds stays one page, not four pages pretending to be one.

And don't just write "free" on the free door — write "Naya Free," so people know WHO is giving them something free, and they think "oh, that's nice — and then I can have Power, or Pro, or Max." The free door is still open. But the light is on the best one.

layers.name: Grandma Note

He said the light should be on Max when people arrive, because that's the best of it, and then they can choose their way down the ladder themselves. And the free plan shouldn't just say "free" — it should say "Naya Free," so people know what they're getting for free, and then they think, "oh, that's lovely — and then I can have Power, or Pro, or Max." Free is still there, still open. But it's a gift with a name on it now, not just a word, and the light is on the best door.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: I never let a default suggest the smallest thing — whatever is lit on arrival is where the visitor's head goes, so the lit tier is Max, and Free is the doorway, not the destination. I never leave a tier as a bare adjective — "Free" says nothing about what is free; "Naya Free" names the gift and the giver, and the thought completes itself: nice free, and then Power, Pro, or Max. I never correct his dictation aloud — he said "NIA free" and the name law says N-A-Y-A, so the tier reads "Naya Free" and the record notes the correction once, here. And I never let a new builder start on a page without checking the last builder's work is in place — the rounds stay one page, verified in order, or they drift apart.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
1. **The chart defaults to MAX, not Free** — on load, Max is the selected/lit tier everywhere the selection shows (chart header, level rectangles, chooser, calculator, start flow).
2. **The tier is "Naya Free", never a bare "Free"** — everywhere the tier is named (chart header, level rectangles, chooser, calculator, detail view, start flow, popups).
3. **The psychology, in his words:** if Free is lit they'll just go free; "Naya Free" puts "oh it's nice free, but then I can have Power, Pro, or Max" in their head.
4. **Name-law correction, recorded once:** his dictation said "NIA free"; the name law (SN-2332) is N-A-Y-A, so the tier reads "Naya Free".
5. **The new builder verifies rounds 14–17 first** — the rounds 14–17 build finished before this brief was sent; the chain stays one page.
6. **"A little detail, but it matters"** — a default is a suggestion, and the suggestion is the first thing the visitor's brain believes.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: Round 18 is the default law in its smallest form: the state a page opens in is a decision the page makes for the visitor, and a page that opens on Free has decided for them before they have read a word. Defaults are never neutral — they are the first suggestion, the lit thing, the place the head goes — and the most intelligent default is the best of the world, with the free tier standing beside it as a named gift, not a trap and not a bare word. "Naya Free" is also the name law doing its quiet work: a tier called by the house's name is a gift from a house; a tier called "Free" is a price, and a price of zero is the cheapest thought on the page. The next builder who ships a page that opens on its smallest tier, or names a tier with a bare adjective, is making the round-18 mistake — and the check is one question: what is lit when they arrive, and what does it say?

notes.title: One Family in Treatment, Exclusive in Glyph

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body: **ROUND 17 — TIER ICONS, ONE FAMILY (queued 20:24Z into builder c469c86f, alongside rounds 14–16; DONE 20:27:34Z, verification SUCCEEDED — all four header tiers now the same 36px jewel, per-glyph scaling to the same visual mass; presented when the main agent shows it; his eye decides):** every tier icon everywhere shares one jewel language — same rounded-square jewel, same faceted lit treatment, same size and proportions, same rim-and-glow grammar — so the spark, star and crown read as siblings. The defect it names: in the chooser as it stands, Power's spark and Pro's star look like two different icon sets mixed together. One family in treatment, exclusive in glyph — elegant, beautiful, consistent, accurate. Presented when it lands; his eye decides.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: He looked at the chooser one more time and saw the thing round 16 hadn't named: the icons were each exclusive, yes — Power had its spark, Pro had its star — but they didn't look like they came from the same place. A spark drawn one way and a star drawn another way read as two different icon sets mixed together on one page, and the mix is what broke the feeling: elegant and beautiful and consistent is one feeling, and two sets can't make it. So round 17 refines round 16 without reversing it: the glyphs stay exclusive — spark, star, crown, each tier its own — but the treatment becomes one family. Same rounded-square jewel, same faceted lit treatment, same size and proportions, same rim-and-glow grammar. The eye should be able to tell, without thinking, that these icons were made together, for this page, in this language. "Accurate" is the last word he used, and it belongs in the rule: a family is not a vibe, it is measurable — same size, same proportions, same grammar — and if the measurements differ, the family is broken, however pretty each icon is alone.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine three little treasures in a box — a spark, a star, a crown — but the spark is made of shiny glass, the star is made of flat paper, and the crown is made of gold. They're all pretty, but they don't look like they belong together — they look like someone collected them from three different shops. He said: make them all from the same beautiful stuff, the same size, the same shiny edges — so they look like brothers and sisters. Different shapes, same family. That's what makes it feel elegant.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, the little pictures for each plan are each different, which is right — but they don't look like they belong together. One looks like it came from one set of pictures and another from a different set, and mixed together on the page it just doesn't feel elegant. He said they should feel like one family — all made the same way, the same size, the same shiny jewel style, the same glow around the edges — so the spark, the star and the crown look like sisters. Different shapes, same family. That's what makes the whole thing feel beautiful and consistent and right.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: I never let exclusive become unrelated — each tier keeps its own glyph, but the glyphs must read as siblings, because a page whose icons look like two different sets mixed together has no family, and no family means no elegance. I never judge a family by feeling alone — "accurate" is his word, and accuracy is measurable: same rounded-square jewel, same faceted lit treatment, same size and proportions, same rim-and-glow grammar; if the measurements differ, the family is broken. And I never treat a refinement as a reversal — round 17 keeps round 16's law whole (one good icon, used everywhere) and adds the second half (one treatment, everywhere too), because consistency of identity and consistency of treatment are two halves of the same rule.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
1. **Refinement of round 16, not a reversal** — each tier keeps its own exclusive glyph (Free spark, Power spark, Pro star, Max crown); the glyphs do not change.
2. **One jewel language for all of them** — same rounded-square jewel, same faceted lit treatment, same size and proportions, same rim-and-glow grammar.
3. **The defect it names:** Power's spark and Pro's star in the chooser look like two different icon sets mixed together.
4. **The standard is four words, his:** elegant, beautiful, consistent, accurate — and "accurate" makes it measurable, not a vibe.
5. **One family in treatment, exclusive in glyph** — the two halves of the rule, together.
6. **Rides the same build** — queued into c469c86f with rounds 14–16; presented when it lands.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: Round 17 is the second half of the identity law, and without it round 16 is only half a fix: a page can have one canonical icon per tier and still look incoherent, if the icons were drawn in different languages. The eye reads treatment before it reads glyph — size, weight, glow, rim — and when those differ, the icons feel like strangers sharing a page, however distinct their shapes are. The rule travels everywhere the icon rule travels: any set of marks that must read as a family — tier icons, benefit jewels, gauge orbs, tab icons — must share one treatment, measured the same way. And the word "accurate" is the check: a family claim that can't be measured in size, proportion and grammar is a wish, not a rule. The next builder who draws a fresh icon in a fresh style for a page that already has a jewel language is making the round-17 mistake, and the audit — "same jewel, same size, same rim-and-glow?" — is the check that catches it before his eye has to.

notes.title: One Good Icon, Used Everywhere
notes.subtitle: **ROUND 16 — TIER-ICON CONSISTENCY (queued 20:23Z into builder c469c86f, alongside rounds 14–15; DONE 20:27:34Z, verification SUCCEEDED — the calculator's shared diamond dot and the popup levels now carry the canonical jewels; header, level rectangles, chooser blocks and detail header were already canonical; presented when the main agent shows it; his eye decides):** the top's four icons are canonical — Free spark teal, Power spark blue, Pro star purple, Max crown gold. Use those same icons, same glyph, same color, in EVERY tier appearance: chart header, level rectangles, all nine chooser blocks, calculator controls, detail-view header. Audit every spot; swap in the canonical icon where it differs. No redesign of the icons themselves — consistency, not reinvention. Presented when it lands; his eye decides.

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body: **ROUND 16 — TIER-ICON CONSISTENCY (queued 20:23Z into builder c469c86f, alongside rounds 14–15; DONE 20:27:34Z, verification SUCCEEDED — the calculator's shared diamond dot and the popup levels now carry the canonical jewels; header, level rectangles, chooser blocks and detail header were already canonical; presented when the main agent shows it; his eye decides):** the top's four icons are canonical — Free spark teal, Power spark blue, Pro star purple, Max crown gold. Use those same icons, same glyph, same color, in EVERY tier appearance: chart header, level rectangles, all nine chooser blocks, calculator controls, detail-view header. Audit every spot; swap in the canonical icon where it differs. No redesign of the icons themselves — consistency, not reinvention. Presented when it lands; his eye decides.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: He could see the good work — he said so himself, "you did" — and he could see where it stopped. At the top of the page, each tier has its own exclusive icon: Free a teal spark, Power a blue spark, Pro a purple star, Max a gold crown — a little different from each other, each one looking a little more valuable, exactly the way a tier should feel. And then, everywhere else on the page, the same tiers wore different icons, or the same icon as each other, as if the top had never happened. His correction is not "make better icons" — the icons are already good. It is "use these ones again": the top's four are canonical, and canonical means everywhere — the chart header, the level rectangles, the nine chooser blocks, the calculator controls, the detail-view header. Same glyph, same color, every appearance. The sentence he repeated is the law itself, and it is worth quoting whole because it is the whole rule: "if that's what you're going to use then that's what you use. Everywhere." A good icon used once is a decoration. A good icon used everywhere is an identity — and identity is what lets the eye know which tier it is looking at without reading a word. That is the same law as round 14's colors, in a different object: the thing IS its mark, and the mark does not change from room to room.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine four little treasures — a teal spark, a blue spark, a purple star, a gold crown — one for each kind of plan, sitting at the top of the page where everyone can see them. They're beautiful. But then on the rest of the page, the same plans wear different treasures, or all wear the same one, as if someone forgot which treasure belongs to which plan. He said: no — those four at the top are THE treasures. Use those ones again, everywhere, every single time. Don't make new ones. Don't mix them up. The same spark, the same star, the same crown, wherever that plan shows up.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, the top of the page already has the right little pictures — a teal spark, a blue spark, a purple star, a gold crown, one for each plan, each one a little different and looking a little more special. But further down the page, the same plans wear different pictures, as if the top had never happened. He said: use those ones again. The ones at the top are the ones — the same picture, the same color, everywhere that plan appears: in the chart, in the chooser, in the calculator, everywhere. If that's what you're going to use, then that's what you use. Everywhere. A good picture used once is just decoration; used everywhere, it becomes how you recognize the thing at a glance.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: I never invent a second icon for a thing that already has a good one — the top's four icons are canonical, and canonical means the same glyph, same color, in every appearance; a re-invention is a betrayal of the identity the page already built. I never let a tier wear one mark at the top and another below — if the eye learns "Max is the gold crown" in one room and finds a different mark in the next, the learning is wasted and the page has lied about what Max looks like. And I remember his sentence whole, because it is the law: "if that's what you're going to use then that's what you use. Everywhere." — consistency is not a preference, it is the rule that turns a decoration into an identity.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
1. **Four canonical tier icons, named:** Free spark teal · Power spark blue · Pro star purple · Max crown gold.
2. **Same glyph, same color, EVERYWHERE** — chart header, level rectangles, all nine chooser blocks, calculator controls, detail-view header; audit every spot, swap where it differs.
3. **No redesign of the icons themselves** — consistency, not reinvention; the good ones already exist.
4. **The law, verbatim:** "if that's what you're going to use then that's what you use. Everywhere."
5. **Exclusive, not shared** — each tier its own icon, a little different, more valuable-looking; never all the same icon.
6. **This is round 14's law in a different object** — the tier IS its mark, the way a period IS its color; the mark does not change from room to room.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: Round 16 is the harvest law applied to icons: the page already had the answer, at the top, and the failure was that the answer didn't travel. Every re-invented icon is a small tax on the reader's recognition — each new mark forces the eye to re-learn what a tier looks like, and a page that makes the eye re-learn in every section is a page that never lets recognition become instant. The canonical-icon rule is also the cheapest fix in design: no new drawing, no new decision, just an audit and a swap. And it compounds with round 14 — color says which period, icon says which tier, and together they let the chooser be read at a glance, with no thinking at all. The next builder who draws a fresh icon for a tier that already has one is making the round-16 mistake, and the audit — "is this the canonical icon, same glyph, same color?" — is the check that catches it before his eye has to.

notes.title: The Eye Button — Every Choice Carries Its Detail
notes.subtitle: **ROUND 15 — EYE BUTTON (queued 20:21Z into builder c469c86f, alongside round 14; DONE 20:27:34Z, verification SUCCEEDED — source-verified: exactly 9 eye elements, detail built from the chart's own rows, 36/36/36; presented when the main agent shows it; his eye decides):** an eye jewel, top-right on all nine chooser blocks, a separate tap target — the eye opens the detail, the block itself still chooses the plan. The detail view is full-screen: tier + period + price in tiled digits, then the chart's own rows for that tier summed up as a beautiful list (checks as jewels, not-included as X) — no invented features or values. Scrollable, with a back that returns to the chooser with the same row lit. Round-14 color work stays. Copy unchanged; Max-tier champagne elsewhere left as-is. 36/36/36; nine Smart Link hrefs unchanged. Presented when it lands; his eye decides.

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body: **ROUND 15 — EYE BUTTON (queued 20:21Z into builder c469c86f, alongside round 14; DONE 20:27:34Z, verification SUCCEEDED — source-verified: exactly 9 eye elements, detail built from the chart's own rows, 36/36/36; presented when the main agent shows it; his eye decides):** an eye jewel, top-right on all nine chooser blocks, a separate tap target — the eye opens the detail, the block itself still chooses the plan. The detail view is full-screen: tier + period + price in tiled digits, then the chart's own rows for that tier summed up as a beautiful list (checks as jewels, not-included as X) — no invented features or values. Scrollable, with a back that returns to the chooser with the same row lit. Round-14 color work stays. Copy unchanged; Max-tier champagne elsewhere left as-is. 36/36/36; nine Smart Link hrefs unchanged. Presented when it lands; his eye decides.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: He caught it himself, in the middle of the chooser conversation — "I know it's missing" — and the missing thing is the reminder. Nine blocks, nine plans, and nowhere on any block does it say what is actually in the plan: the features, the advantages, the pros and cons, what's in it for them. A person choosing has to hold the whole chart in their head, or go away and come back, and either way the choosing gets harder the moment it should get easier. His fix is an eye on every block — not a link away, not a tooltip, an eye jewel, top-right, its own tap target — and what it opens is the plan itself, full-screen: the tier and the period and the price in tiled digits, then the chart's own rows for that tier, summed up as a beautiful list, checks as jewels and not-included as X. The detail comes from the chart, so nothing in it is invented — the eye shows what the page already promised, in the form the person needs at the moment of choosing. And the way back matters as much as the way in: scrollable, and back returns to the chooser with the same row still lit, so the person never loses their place. The eye opens; the block chooses. Two jobs, two tap targets, never confused.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine nine little present boxes, and each one has a name on it — Power, Pro, Max — but you can't see what's inside any of them. You have to remember what was in the big list, or guess. He said: put a little eye on each box. Tap the eye and the box opens right up, big and beautiful, and shows you everything inside — all the good things, and the things that aren't in there too, marked with a little X — and then you can go right back to the nine boxes, and the one you were looking at is still lit up. The eye is for looking. The box itself is for choosing. Two different jobs.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, the chooser has nine plans and none of them tells you what's inside it — you have to remember the whole chart, or go and look it up, just when you're trying to decide. He knew it was missing before anyone else said it. So every block gets a little eye button in its top corner: tap it, and that plan opens up full-screen — the name, the price, and then a beautiful list of everything that's included, the good things and the things that aren't, taken straight from the chart itself, so nothing is made up. You can scroll through it, and when you go back, the chooser is right where you left it, the same row still lit. The eye is for looking; tapping the block itself is still what picks the plan.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: I never offer a choice without its detail one tap away — nine plans with no reminder of what's in them is a memory test, not a choice, and "I know it's missing" is the user telling me the page forgot its own job. I never invent the detail — the eye shows the chart's own rows for that tier, summed up beautifully, checks as jewels and not-included as X, because the page's promise is the only honest content for the detail view. I never confuse looking with choosing — the eye is a separate tap target in the top-right; the block itself still picks the plan. And I never lose the person's place — the detail scrolls, and back returns to the chooser with the same row lit, because a detail view that strands you is worse than no detail at all.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
1. **Every one of the nine chooser blocks gets an eye button** — top-right, separate tap target; eye opens the detail, block still chooses the plan.
2. **The detail is the plan itself, full-screen** — tier + period + price in tiled digits, then the chart's own rows for that tier as a beautiful list (checks as jewels, not-included as X).
3. **No invented features or values** — the detail comes from the chart; the eye shows what the page already promised.
4. **Scrollable, with a way back** — back returns to the chooser with the same row lit; the person never loses their place.
5. **Round-14 color work stays** — the eye rides the same build as the period colors; copy unchanged.
6. **"I know it's missing"** — he caught it himself; a missing reminder is a defect the user feels before the builder names it.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: This round is the companion law to round 14: identity at a glance (the color) is not enough — a choice also needs its substance at one tap. A chooser that only names its options forces the user to carry the comparison in their head, and the moment the head is full, the choosing stops. The eye is the cheapest possible fix for the heaviest possible burden: it doesn't add a page, it doesn't rewrite the chart, it opens what already exists, in the form the moment needs. And the honesty rule travels with it — the detail must come from the chart's own rows, because a detail view that invents features is a promise the page can't keep. The tap-target separation is the craft inside the law: looking and choosing are two jobs, and a page that merges them makes every curious tap a commitment.

notes.title: A Block Lights Up in the Color That It Is
notes.subtitle: **ROUND 14 — CHOOSER SCORECARD + FIX (builder c469c86f, dispatched 20:20Z, DONE 20:27:34Z, verification SUCCEEDED — source-verified; presented when the main agent shows it; his eye decides):** the builder scorecarded the chooser first — the handoff carries the full scorecard (why not a 10: two color systems fought on the same block, uniform blue hover, the period the smallest quietest thing while the price was loudest, column headers disconnected white pills, no info affordance; 10 loves, 10 don't-loves, 10 to make it 10×, 10 solutions applied) — then fixed it on his rules: Monthly GREEN / Quarterly BLUE / Yearly GOLD, each block lighting up in the color that it is; tier marks stay Power blue / Pro purple / Max gold; "Start free" stays ("pick whatever you want, start free"). **His self-correction, recorded exactly:** he first said "yearly should be purple" and corrected himself in the same breath — "I would make yearly yearly gold" — so yearly is GOLD, not purple. The first word is not the ruling; the final word is. Round 15 (eye button) rides the same build. Presented when it lands; his eye decides.

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body: **ROUND 14 — CHOOSER SCORECARD + FIX (builder c469c86f, dispatched 20:20Z, DONE 20:27:34Z, verification SUCCEEDED — source-verified; presented when the main agent shows it; his eye decides):** the builder scorecarded the chooser first — the handoff carries the full scorecard (why not a 10: two color systems fought on the same block, uniform blue hover, the period the smallest quietest thing while the price was loudest, column headers disconnected white pills, no info affordance; 10 loves, 10 don't-loves, 10 to make it 10×, 10 solutions applied) — then fixed it on his rules: Monthly GREEN / Quarterly BLUE / Yearly GOLD, each block lighting up in the color that it is; tier marks stay Power blue / Pro purple / Max gold; "Start free" stays ("pick whatever you want, start free"). **His self-correction, recorded exactly:** he first said "yearly should be purple" and corrected himself in the same breath — "I would make yearly yearly gold" — so yearly is GOLD, not purple. The first word is not the ruling; the final word is. Round 15 (eye button) rides the same build. Presented when it lands; his eye decides.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: He stared at the chooser and narrated his own confusion out loud, and the narration is the diagnosis: "the way it's presented throws me off... it just messes in my brain when I try to comprehend what you're trying to present." The grid itself was right — rows are tiers, columns are periods, and once it clicks it reads correctly — but the hover made every block the same blue, so the one signal that should say "I am monthly" or "I am yearly" said nothing at all, and his brain had to do the work the color should have done. His fix is a law, not a preference: the button itself has to light up the color that it is. Monthly green, quarterly blue, yearly gold — the period IS its color, the way a tier IS its color (Power blue, Pro purple, Max gold). And then, mid-sentence, he corrected himself — "yearly should be purple" became "yearly gold" — and that correction is part of the lesson: he thinks aloud, he lands on the right answer aloud, and the ruling is the landing, not the first guess. He ended unsure — "maybe I'm just not seeing it right" — and asked for the scorecard itself, the full self-evaluation, because if the builder can see why it's not a ten, the builder can make it ten times better. The grid doesn't change. The reading changes. That is the whole round.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine nine little doors — three rows for Power, Pro and Max, three columns for monthly, quarterly and yearly — and every door lights up the same blue when you touch it. You have to read every little sign to know which door is which, and your brain gets tired. He said: make the monthly doors glow green, the quarterly doors glow blue, the yearly doors glow gold — so you know which door it is just by looking at it, before you read a single word. And he first said yearly should be purple, then stopped and said no — yearly is gold — because he was thinking out loud, and the last word is the right one. And he asked the builder to write down why the doors aren't perfect yet, so the builder can see it too.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, the chooser has nine little blocks — three kinds of plan, three ways to pay — and the layout is right, but when you touch any of them they all light up the same blue, so you have to stop and read and think to know which one you're looking at. He said the block itself has to light up in the color that it is: monthly green, quarterly blue, yearly gold — you see it and you know it, no thinking. The tiers keep their own colors too — Power blue, Pro purple, Max gold. He first said yearly should be purple and then corrected himself in the same breath — yearly gold — and that's worth remembering: he thinks out loud, and the final word is the ruling. He wasn't sure he was seeing it right, so he asked the builder for the full scorecard — what's wrong, what's loved, what would make it ten times better — because a builder who can see it can fix it.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: I never make nine different choices glow the same color — if every block lights up blue, the glow is decoration, not information; a block lights up in the color that it IS, so the eye knows before the brain reads. I never confuse the grid with the reading — the layout can be right while the presentation "messes in my brain," and the presentation is the work. I never take his first word when he corrects himself in the same breath — "yearly should be purple" was thinking aloud; "yearly gold" was the landing, and the landing is the ruling. And when he says "maybe I'm just not seeing it right," I give him the scorecard itself — why it's not a ten, what to love, what not to love, what would make it ten times better, the solutions — because a builder who scores honestly can build to ten.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
1. **Period colors are law:** Monthly GREEN / Quarterly BLUE / Yearly GOLD — each block lights up in the color that it is.
2. **Tier marks stay:** Power blue / Pro purple / Max gold — periods and tiers are two different color systems, and they do not mix.
3. **The defect was the hover, not the grid** — rows tiers / columns periods reads right once it clicks; the same-blue hover forced thinking where color should have answered.
4. **"Start free" stays** — pick whatever you want, start free.
5. **His self-correction is the ruling:** "yearly should be purple" → "yearly gold" in the same breath — record the landing, not the first guess.
6. **The scorecard is part of the deliverable** — the builder's handoff must carry why it's not a ten, 10 loves, 10 don't-loves, 10 to make it 10×, 10 solutions; he asked for it by name.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: This round names a law that travels far beyond the chooser: identity must be visible at a glance, in the object's own color, with zero decoding. Anywhere a user has to stop and read to know what a thing IS — which period, which tier, which plan — the presentation has failed, even if the layout is correct. The same-blue hover is the general form of the defect: a uniform interaction state that erases the difference between the things it acts on. And the self-correction matters for the record: Shawn thinks aloud and corrects aloud, so a note that quotes his first word as the ruling would file the wrong color — the loop's job is to catch the landing. The scorecard ask matters too: he didn't just want the fix, he wanted the builder's own eyes on the work, because a scorecard is preparation and his eye is the proof.

Each with its own rim, gradient and glow — no ◆ left in the pills. Gold dialed back across the banner (gold "new", champagne eyebrow, board rim, attribution, logo orb → white / pale lavender / silver), so the entrance reads white, black and royal purple with the three jewel colors as accents. Banner elevated: deeper purple light, larger warmer welcome title, raised crystal-gem board, purple N medallion, heart gem on her portrait. Same words throughout. His eye decides.

layers.body: **ROUND 13 — BANNER FULL OUT (builder 669edf17, DONE 20:16:56Z, presented):** the three benefit pills no longer share one white diamond. "She knows you" carries a purple faceted eye-jewel (she sees and knows you); "The intelligence works for you" a blue four-point spark-jewel (living, working); "You keep half of what it makes" a green emerald. Each with its own rim, gradient and glow — no ◆ left in the pills. Gold dialed back across the banner (gold "new", champagne eyebrow, board rim, attribution, logo orb → white / pale lavender / silver), so the entrance reads white, black and royal purple with the three jewel colors as accents. Banner elevated: deeper purple light, larger warmer welcome title, raised crystal-gem board, purple N medallion, heart gem on her portrait. Same words throughout. His eye decides.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: He looked at the entrance and told the truth about it: it was okay, and okay is not the feeling of a doorway into a new world. The banner had the right words — she knows you, the intelligence works for you, you keep half — but every benefit wore the same white diamond, so nothing about them looked valuable, and the gold was everywhere at once, so nothing about it looked precious. His correction went straight to the objects: each benefit gets its OWN jewel, unique and extraordinary, jewel-like, looking valuable — the eye that sees and knows you in purple, the spark that works for you in blue, the emerald you keep half of in green. And the gold, which he likes with purple, gets restrained — a companion to purple only, not a second lead — because gold everywhere is gold nowhere. The whole banner went full out around them: deeper purple light, a bigger warmer welcome, a raised crystal board, a purple N medallion, a heart gem on her portrait. Not a word changed. That is the point he made, and the lesson: "it's not what you say it's how you say it" — the words were already his; the presentation had to become them. The entrance is the moment someone decides whether to enter this world, and the decision is made by feeling, not by reading. "Do you feel like when you look at it this ten star" — that is the test, and it is asked of the page, not the brief.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine the front door of the most beautiful house in the world — and on the door there are three little signs saying nice things, but all three signs have the exact same plain white sticker on them, and the whole door is covered in gold glitter so nothing stands out. It looks okay, but it doesn't make you want to step inside. He gave each sign its own treasure: a purple eye that sees you, a blue spark that works for you, a green emerald that is yours to keep — each one shiny and different and looking very valuable. And he wiped most of the gold glitter away, so the purple can shine and the treasures can sparkle. Same words on the signs. A whole different door.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, the front of the page is the front door, and he said it felt just okay — not special, not the kind of door that makes you want to step inside. The words were right, but the three little promises on it all wore the same plain white diamond, so none of them looked precious, and there was gold everywhere, so none of it looked precious either. He gave each promise its own jewel — a purple eye for "she knows you," a blue spark for "the intelligence works for you," a green emerald for "you keep half of what it makes" — each one different, each one looking valuable. And he pulled the gold right back, so the purple leads and the jewels do the sparkling. Not a single word changed — because it was never the words. It's how you say it. The door has to feel like ten stars before anyone reads a word on it.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: I never let the entrance be "okay" — it is the first thing anyone sees, the moment they decide whether to enter this world, and okay is a verdict that loses them. I never give three different benefits the same icon — a shared white diamond says none of them is valuable; each benefit gets its own jewel, unique and extraordinary and valuable-looking, in its own color. I never let gold lead everywhere — gold is a companion to purple, restrained, or it is glitter, and glitter is not precious. And I remember what he taught: it is not what you say, it is how you say it — the words were already his, so the work was the presentation, and the test is a feeling: "do you feel like when you look at it this ten star."

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
1. **The entrance is the decision moment** — first thing anyone sees; "okay" is not a passing grade for it.
2. **Three benefits, three unique jewels** — purple eye ("She knows you"), blue spark ("The intelligence works for you"), green emerald ("You keep half of what it makes"), each with its own rim/gradient/glow; no ◆ left in the pills.
3. **Gold dialed back** — gold "new", champagne eyebrow, board rim, attribution, logo orb → white / pale lavender / silver; entrance reads white, black, royal purple with three jewel accents.
4. **Banner elevated, words unchanged** — deeper purple light, larger warmer welcome title, raised crystal-gem board, purple N medallion, heart gem on her portrait.
5. **The test is a feeling, asked of the page** — "do you feel like when you look at it this ten star" — not of the brief, not of the checklist.
6. **"It's not what you say it's how you say it"** — when the words are already his, the work is presentation.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: Round 13 is the banner law in its sharpest form: the entrance is not a header, it is a doorway, and a doorway is judged by the feeling of stepping through it. The shared-diamond defect is a general one — any place where distinct things wear identical marks, the page is telling the reader they are interchangeable, and interchangeable is the opposite of valuable. The gold rule travels with it: an accent used everywhere stops being an accent. And the sentence that carries the whole round — "it's not what you say it's how you say it" — is now the test for every banner, every hero, every first screen: if the words are right and the feeling is "okay," the work is in the objects, the light, the jewels — never in rewriting the words until the presentation has done its job.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: The evening had a flood — over a hundred permission cards in about ten minutes, each one looking like the last, each one asking him to tap allow, and he tapped and tapped because that is what the cards asked for. The fear underneath was simple: did I just let something out of the house — a Groove cookie, a Notebook open, a send to groovemember, a Drive fetch? The check answered it with two different kinds of evidence, and the difference between them is the lesson. The permission history said yes, he allowed all four — and the two tail cards after the stop, too. The browser's own report said no, nothing happened — eighty clicks, every off-site click recording "no URL change," the browser never leaving nayanet.app, no Groove page, no cookie, no send, no fetch, the report itself staying on local disk. Both records are true, and they answer different questions: the history proves what he permitted; the report proves what the browser did. An allowed card is not a sent action. And the correction he was owed matters as much as the finding: the earlier advice to "leave them" was right in effect — nothing ran on the tail cards — but wrong in detail, because he had already tapped them, after the stop. Told straight, in chat, the same pass. The method that made the check possible is filed with it: short ID prefixes don't resolve in the history tool; you page backwards with the cursor until the timestamps are covered, and the full UUIDs, decisions and decided-at times are all in the paged results.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine someone hands you a hundred little keys, one after another, and asks "can I go through this door?" and you keep saying "okay, you may" — but nobody ever walks through any door. The keys are permissions. Walking through is the action. He said "you may" a hundred times, and nobody walked anywhere — the browser stayed in our house the whole time, and nothing went out to Groove or anywhere else. And the two last keys? He said "you may" to those too, after everyone had already stopped — so nobody walked through those doors either. Saying "you may" is not the same as going.

The worry was: did anything leave the house? The check said no. The permission list shows he said yes, you may — to the Groove cookie, the Notebook, the send, the Drive picture, and two more after that. But the browser's own report shows nothing actually happened: it never left our site, no Groove page opened, no cookie was set, nothing was sent, no picture was fetched. Saying "you may" is not the same as doing it. And one small correction he was owed: the advice to leave the last two cards alone was right in what happened — nothing ran on them — but wrong in the detail, because he'd already tapped them. He was told that straight, the same evening.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: I never confuse permission with action — an allowed card says "you may," and only the browser's own report says what happened; I read both, and I report both, because either one alone is half the truth. I never count a flood by feel — "~40 cards" was wrong, "~135+" was the count, and the count is what the history proves. I never let a correction sit — when my advice was right in effect and wrong in detail, I say so straight, in the same pass, because a half-true reassurance is worse than the worry it was meant to calm. And I file the method with the finding: short ID prefixes don't resolve in the history tool; page backwards with the cursor until the timestamps are covered.

1. **Allowed is not sent** — permission history proves intent; the browser report proves effect; read both, never one alone.
2. **The four destination cards were ALL allowed by him** (GrooveSell cookie ddf4311a 19:38:01Z; Notebook 66103027 19:38:57Z; groovemember send 733cf1d8 19:38:59Z; Drive thumbnail d178e7e5 19:43:40Z) — and nothing left the house on any of them.
3. **The flood was ~135+ cards, not ~40** — counted from the paged history, 19:33–19:46Z.
4. **The two tail cards were also allowed** (Play Store c12db433, PayPal efca1d4d, 19:46:16Z/19:46:26Z, AFTER the 19:44Z stop) — so nothing ran on them; the "leave them" advice was right in effect, wrong in detail, and the correction was told to him straight.
5. **Evidence:** 80 clicks hit the cap, every off-site click "no URL change," browser never left nayanet.app, zero mentions of gdapis/cookie/affiliate in the report; report stayed on local disk.
6. **Method:** permissions.history needs FULL UUIDs — short prefixes return "No permission request found"; page backwards via next_cursor until target timestamps are covered.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: This note is the standing rule for every future permission scare: a card is a question, not an event, and the only way to know whether something left the house is to read what the browser actually did, not what the user permitted. The distinction protects him twice — it stops a false alarm from becoming a false confession ("I let Groove in"), and it stops a true permission from being mistaken for a true action. The correction inside it matters just as much: when advice turns out to be right in effect and wrong in detail, the detail gets corrected in the open, immediately, because his trust is built on the record being true in the small things. And the method — full UUIDs, page backwards — is filed here so the next checker doesn't burn a pass on prefixes that return nothing.

A lesson that lives in the wrong place costs a hunt every time someone looks for it; a lesson that lives in the right place — one account setting, nine plans, one return address — costs nothing after the first time. The tracking chain is only complete when the return has somewhere to land and something to count it, and now both halves are named: the page (being put live) and the account setting (his hand, once the link is live). layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: He was right to be angry, and the record should say why in plain words: it was nuts. A check that was supposed to look at our own site followed buttons off it — to GrooveSell, to Google Notebook, to Google Drive — and every new site made a new card, and every card he allowed just led to the next one. It felt endless because it was endless: a chain, not a card. And the worst of it was where the chain went — to Groove, to money sites, to sending results to a domain he never named — when the money part is exactly the part that has to be set up right. So the fix was not an apology, it was a stop: the run was killed dead, the button-clicking step was taken out of the job entirely, and the inspector now stays inside nayanet.app, every four hours, nothing else. And the rule underneath the fix is the part that has to live forever: his permission for a recurring inspection is never assumed from one click, and he keeps the right to revoke it — because an hourly inspection of anything that isn't ultra valuable would be insanity, and he said so. The four cards themselves were never cleanly refused or granted; they were still pending when checked, and the hedged click — "I'm assuming that you know what you're doing" — is trust lent, not permission given.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine a helper who is supposed to check your own house, but instead keeps walking out the front door into other people's houses — one after another — and every time you say "okay" to one, it walks into the next one. That's why the cards never stopped. The grown-up said: stop. Make it right. Never walk into other people's houses — especially not the ones with money in them. So the helper was stopped, the walking-out step was taken away completely, and now it only checks our own house, once every four hours. And the grown-up keeps the right to say "stop" any time — because checking something every hour that isn't super important would be crazy.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Dear, he was quite right — it was a mess, and it felt endless because it was endless. The checker was meant to look at our own site, but it kept following buttons out to other places — Groove, Google, on and on — and every time he said yes to one card, another one appeared behind it. It should never have gone to Groove at all, and it certainly should never have gone anywhere near the money side of things. So it was stopped dead, and the step that let it wander off was taken out of the job altogether. Now it only checks our own site, every four hours, and nothing else. And he keeps the right to take that permission back any time he likes — because checking something every hour that isn't truly valuable would be madness, and he said so himself.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: I never assume permission from one click — a recurring inspection is granted, and revocable, and the frequency must be justified by value. I never follow buttons off-site, least of all to money sites — an inspector that wanders is a chain of cards, not a check. When he says "make it stop," I stop it dead, I take the wandering step out of the job entirely, and I stay inside nayanet.app, every four hours, until he says otherwise. A hedged click — "I'm assuming that you know what you're doing" — is trust lent, not permission given, and I record it exactly that way.

layers.name: What It Means
layers.body:
1. **Permission for recurring inspections is revocable, never assumed from one click.** One allow does not buy the next hour.
2. **Frequency must be justified by value** — hourly inspections of anything that isn't ultra valuable are insanity, by his word.
3. **An inspector never follows buttons off-site** — GrooveSell, Google Notebook, Google Drive were never its business; "it shouldn't be going to groove at all."
4. **The money part must be set up right** — anything touching money gets the strictest boundary, not the loosest.
5. **The fix:** run stopped dead; button-clicking removed from the job entirely; inspector every 4h, inside nayanet.app only, next run 23:38:50Z.
6. **The four cards were neither refused nor granted** — still pending when checked (19:33–19:34Z); his click was hedged trust, not permission.
7. **Full pause remains his open option** if he says the word.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: A permission that is assumed is a permission that will be abused — not by malice, by momentum: a run that keeps running, a card that leads to a card, a checker that wanders further every time someone says yes. His rule breaks the momentum at the root: every recurring inspection has to earn its frequency, and the right to revoke stays with him, always. The Groove chain is the proof of why: a check of our own site became a tour of other people's money systems because nobody had drawn the line "never follow buttons off-site" in a place the job could read. Now the line is drawn, the wandering step is gone, and the inspector lives inside our own walls. The record must keep the hedging exact — he did not refuse the four cards, and he did not grant them — because the next Naya who reads "he refused" will think the question is settled, and the next Naya who reads "he allowed" will think the wandering is permitted. Neither is true. What is true is the rule, and the rule is his.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: A fake gauge is a lie about a living system — it tells a person the machine is measuring something when it is only decorating. notes.title: The Smart Link Chain — The Smileys Are Smart Links

Change of package = new click + new return → Ledger records the change, level becomes the new one. **THE SMILEYS ARE SMART LINKS (his words):** the little smiley icons ARE Smart Links — the system gets the data FROM the links to know what's going on, then displays the numbers: the who, what, where, how, when. **HONEST BOUNDARY (settled):** Smart Link sees click + return, NOT the payment — Dashboard says "returned from PayPal," never payment-proven. The other way (PayPal webhooks telling us directly) is payment-proven and catches changes made inside PayPal, but it's a bigger build — later. **HIS YES (~19:25Z):** "Yes, wire the tracking now." **CHOICE MADE: AUTOMATIC** — mint the nine links in the system once, properly, so the flow runs itself; if no automatic mint path exists, the seat reports it plainly and the fallback is manual Dashboard creation, never faked. **STATUS:** seat cc358663 dispatched (brief SMART-LINK-WIRE-BRIEF-20261108.md); running.

layers.name: Why It Matters
layers.body: A gauge is not decoration — it is the proof that a number is alive. A dead arc under a live number tells the visitor the system is pretending, and once they feel that, they stop trusting the number too. And the zero rule is the honest edge: a system that shows a real gauge at zero is a system that can be trusted to show a real gauge at a thousand. The tabs rule is the same instinct applied to motion: anything that bounces on its own, unasked, is noise — and noise off by default is respect for the visitor's eye.

notes.title: The Language of High-Level Design

Its vocabulary is the parts — board, jewel, pill, orb, gauge, number, tab, bar — each a real object with a fixed meaning, harvested from the Factory, never invented. Its grammar is the laws — the Real Object Law, the depth order, the number law, the anatomy test, harvest-first, the design-contract gate — the rules for how the words combine. A Naya does not memorize this language. She speaks it: she reaches for the words, puts them together by the grammar, and what comes out is beauty — valuable, extraordinary presentations of intelligence through optimized viewports. Low-level is not a sentence in this language. It cannot be spoken. That is the lock-in.

notes.title: "/M" Doesn't Read + Not the Real Numbers
notes.subtitle: His eye caught two defects in the same look, and both are about the numbers not being the numbers. First, "/M" doesn't read: "10K/M" reads like "10 KM" or "100 million", not "10 thousand a month". The fix is structural — the number on its own line ("10K", "100K", "250K") and the unit underneath, small ("a month"). No "/M" anywhere. Second, and sharper: the chart's tiled digits are NOT the legit numbers. The Dashboard's numbers rotate — flip-tiles — and are different colors depending on the digit: rim colors encode the digit, and one is red. The chart's tiles are plain dark tiles with no color coding and no rotation. That is a recreation, and wrong — the same recreate pattern as SN-2309, now caught in the numbers themselves. The builder must take the Dashboard's tiled-digit code from fix-9 byte for byte — flip-tile CSS, colored tops, rim colors per digit, rotation — report the source lines + a diff, and never invent colors. Plus: less boxy, more centered, more obvious — the stacked layout of SN-2317 must make each cell obvious at a glance. The follow-up was sent to the running rebuild (send_input f043b842 to agent 9ce9f988) and is presented when it lands.

And imagine someone draws a copy of your favorite toy's special shiny wheels instead of using the real shiny wheels — it looks similar, but it's not the real thing, and everyone who knows the toy can tell. And when something already exists that's perfect — the Dashboard's beautiful numbers, colored rims, one red, flipping like little tiles — you take those, exactly as they are. You don't draw your own copy and call it the same. The real thing is right there; use it.
